results.desc: A nurse, 41, on her third year of double shifts. Not in conflict with anyone, just exhausted and numb. She prays less than she used to.

answers.wanted: Same, but it's wearing me down more and more
Worn out and numb together; she'd want to pick both, or 'Running on empty'
Work, and just getting through each shift (not money or what's next)
I barely see anyone outside work / I'm too tired for people
Honestly, I haven't been reaching out much (the distance is on my side, not His)
I'm so tired. / I don't really know what to say anymore.

friction.note: Having to pick one word between 'Worn out' and 'Numb' is hard for her. Those two often go together, so it should allow two picks or have one option that joins them.

'Work, money or what's next' puts three different worries in one option. Her worry is the grind of work, not money or the future, so the option feels only half about her. Nothing covers 'just getting through the days'.
There is no option for 'I've pulled away' or 'too tired for people'. 'Fine' is technically true but says nothing about her situation.

Every option describes what God is doing (far, displeased, silent, quiet). None lets her say the drift is on her side ('I've stopped reaching out'), and someone who prays less would notice that straight away. 'Displeased with me' feels heavy and leading.

The options range from lament to courtroom language. 'Why do they get away with it?' and 'You decide who's right' feel oddly specific and push toward an enemies story. There is no 'I'm tired' or 'I don't know what to say' for someone who is numb and barely praying. Offering nothing that honest is the quickest way to make her feel boxed in.

'About the same' is accurate, but it misses the slow wearing-down of a long stretch. 'Something hard just ended' and 'Something new just began' feel like they come from a different kind of list than the three before them.

results.overall: The quiz was quick and mostly kind, and the first two questions fitted her well. From 'feel' onward she kept picking the nearest answer rather than the true one. The God and 'say' questions assume she is in active conversation with Him, or up against someone, so a tired, numb nurse who has quietly drifted never finds herself on the list.

verdict.why: Line 1 is the only one that fits her life. She isn't pleading with God about anything; she is worn down, running on empty and flat. "Worn you down" and "listless" describe three years of double shifts well. Psalm 102:4 ("withered like grass; I even forget to eat my bread") reads like a nurse skipping meals on a shift, so she would feel seen, not boxed in. Line 2 would feel wrong, because she prays less and isn't reaching for words to plead with. She would tap "Yes" on line 1 without needing the fallback.
verdict.wouldHurt: "Poor" is easy to read as short of money, which isn't her problem; "drained" or "spent" would land better. "You need comfort" assumes she is reaching for something, but she feels numb, not hungry for comfort. A line like "and you can't even tell what you need" would fit her better. In the full psalm, 102:10 ("because of Your indignation and wrath") could land as blame for a woman who already feels guilty that she prays less, as if the exhaustion were God's anger. A short note beside it would help. The later verses about Zion being rebuilt may feel far from her own life.
verdict.theirSituation: She has been worn out for years by the double shifts and has gone numb. She isn't in conflict with anyone and isn't grieving or scared, and she has drifted from prayer without any crisis behind it.

results.desc: A man, 35, who had an affair. His wife found out last week. He is ashamed and wants to make it right.

answers.wanted: Something hard just started / Everything just fell apart. It isn't a slow slide. It blew up last week, and 'Something new just began' sounds like good news.
Ashamed (or Guilty). That is the one word that fits, and it isn't there.
Hurt by me / Rightly angry with me. My wife has pulled away, but not because she's 'hard to be around' or 'against me'. I caused it.

friction.note: There is no word for shame or guilt. For anyone who has done wrong, that is the most obvious feeling, so 'Heavy' has to stand in for it.
None of the options fits a sudden blow-up that just started. 'Getting worse' suggests a slow decline, and the one option about a fresh change, 'Something new just began', sounds positive.

Almost every negative option blames the other people ('Against me', 'Talking behind my back', 'Hard to be around'). There is no way to say 'I hurt them, and they're right to be angry.' A remorseful person gets pushed into sounding like a victim or picking 'Far away' as a dodge.
'Something I've done' and 'Someone I care about' both fit, since the wife is on his mind as much as the wrongdoing. A person could reasonably tap either one, and the result could swing on it.

'Why do they get away with it?' and 'You decide who's right' are aimed at people who have been wronged. Next to them the list tilts toward grievance. There is also nothing about wanting to make things right or asking for a way forward, such as 'Show me how to fix this.'
'A sense that God is warning me' sounds churchy and a bit preachy. 'Something I did' fits, but it's thin: nothing separates 'I did it and it's over' from 'I hurt someone and I'm trying to repair it.'

results.overall: The quiz caught the core of his situation easily: really hard, something I did, God displeased, I'm sorry. But the emotional vocabulary around it (feelings, how things are changing, the people) is built for someone who has been wronged, so a man who is ashamed of what he did keeps having to pick near-misses or answers that blame someone else.

verdict.why: Line 1 is exactly where he is: he did wrong, he knows it, he is ashamed and he wants to come back. It is plain and doesn't accuse him. It names no affair, so he isn't boxed in, and he can still say yes to it at once. Psalm 51 is the psalm David wrote after his adultery with Bathsheba, so the result fits him closely. Its opening ("blot out my transgressions") and its turn ("wash me, and I will be whiter than snow") give him words for confession and a real hope of being made clean. Athanasius's advice ("you are turning back, and you are asking for mercy") treats him as someone repenting, not as someone condemned. He would feel seen, and the result would help him rather than shame him further.

results.desc: A 16-year-old being mocked at school by a group for being a Christian. His parents do not know.

answers.wanted: Alone, or Embarrassed. Angry is part of it, but mostly I feel alone and kind of humiliated.
People at school, or Other people. 'Someone' sounds like one person, and it's a group.
Making fun of me. 'Against me' is a bit dramatic, and 'Talking behind my back' is wrong because they say it to my face.
A group at school. 'A whole group of people' sounds like a mob, but it's the nearest one.
Being laughed at, or Having to see them every day. They say it to my face, so 'what they're saying about me' sounds like gossip.

friction.note: There's no word for lonely, embarrassed or ashamed. For a teenager who's being mocked, those are the main feelings, and none of the nine words covers them.
'Someone in my life' is singular, so anyone dealing with a group has no clear option. 'Work, money or what's next' reads as an adult's list. A teen would expect 'School'.

The only negative options are 'Against me' and 'Talking behind my back'. Being mocked to your face falls between them. 'Against me' also sounds paranoid to a 16-year-old. A milder middle option like 'Mean to me' or 'Making fun of me' is missing.
'Displeased with me' and 'Clearly at work' sound churchy. A teen wouldn't use either phrase.
'You decide who's right.' makes no sense as something you'd say to God. It reads like a legal term. 'Why do they get away with it?' is a strong nudge toward a particular kind of result.
'People with power over me' is vague. A teen might read it as teachers or parents. 'A whole group of people' sounds like a crowd or a mob rather than a group of classmates.
Asking straight out 'Is your faith part of it?' gives away that the quiz is steering toward persecution psalms. It isn't disguised.

'What they might be planning' and 'Not knowing what they'll do next' sound like a thriller or a stalking case, not school bullying. None of the options covers being laughed at, the embarrassment, or having nobody to tell. For this kid, keeping it secret from his parents is a big part of it, and the quiz has no way to pick that up.

results.overall: It was quick, and the first few taps felt fine. But the questions about people are written for adults dealing with enemies or office politics, so a kid being mocked at school had to settle for 'near enough' answers four times. Most of the words didn't sound like him, especially 'Against me', 'Displeased with me' and 'You decide who's right'.

verdict.why: I'd say yes to line 1, because its second half is my life. A group at school mocks me for being a Christian, and "people keep throwing it at you" names that without making it sound dramatic. "Where is your God?" isn't word for word what they say. They're more likely to say "your imaginary friend" or "you actually believe that?" Still, it's the same jab, and when Psalm 42 says men ask it "all day long", that sounds like school: every day, in the same place, from the same people. The first half is what makes me pause. "You long for God with everything in you" feels bigger than I'd say about myself at 16. I'm trying to hold on to my faith, not burning with longing, so it flatters me a little. I'd still tap yes because the taunting part is so exact. The turn at 42:5, "Why are you downcast, O my soul? … Put your hope in God", gives me something I could actually say to myself in the hallway. Athanasius's advice, "don't be troubled", comfort your soul with hope, is gentle and doesn't lecture me. Line 2 (plead with God, Psalm 5) is too generic, and I'd pass on it. The fallback would also work if I got there: "It's weighing on me, and it won't lift" leads to Psalm 42 anyway. What the quiz doesn't see is that I'm carrying this alone because my parents don't know, but nothing in the result makes that worse.
verdict.wouldHurt: "My tears have been my food both day and night" and "long for God with everything in you" could feel like they overstate me. A teenage boy might wince at being described as crying all day, even if that's close to the truth. Nothing says what to do if the mocking gets worse, or that telling someone you trust is fine. That doesn't wound, but it's a gap for a kid who is keeping this secret.
verdict.theirSituation: A teenager being mocked at school for his faith and hiding it from his parents. The taunting in line 1 is his life, but the "longing with everything in you" part is bigger than how he sees himself.

results.desc: A widow, 72, whose husband of 50 years died four months ago. She is not angry at anyone; she is grieving.

answers.wanted: Something like 'A little easier some days' or 'Still raw'. Four months in, it's not worse or better, just different. 'Something hard just ended' nearly pulled me because my marriage ended, but that isn't what it means.
Lonely. That's the word. The house is empty. 'Heavy' is near enough, but lonely is what a widow would reach for first.
Something like 'Holding me, but I can't feel it much' or 'There, but I'm too tired to reach'. 'Near, but quiet' is close enough.
'Hold me' or 'Be with me', or 'Take care of him for me.' 'I miss You' looked like it was meant for me, but I miss HIM, not God, so it felt wrong to tap. 'Help' is the nearest.

friction.note: 'Something hard just ended' is confusing for a widow: her marriage did just end, so she might tap it and then get 'What was it?' with options like 'People who were against me', which would feel cold and wrong. The list mixes directions (worse/same/better) with events (ended/began), so it's hard to tell what's being asked.
No 'Lonely' or 'Sad'. Those are the most common words for grief. 'Heavy' is poetic and some older people wouldn't say it about themselves.
'Someone or something I've lost' fits, but lumping a husband of 50 years in with 'something' makes it feel smaller. Just 'Someone I've lost' would read as kinder.

Three of the seven options are about enemies ('Against me', 'Talking behind my back', 'Hard to be around'). For an ordinary grieving person the list feels built for somebody else. 'Far away, or gone' could get tapped by a widow meaning her husband, which would muddle the result.

'I miss You' is ambiguous. A grieving person reads 'miss' and thinks of the one she lost, then sees the capital Y and feels she has to pick something else. 'Why do they get away with it?' and 'You decide who's right.' read like lines from a specific psalm, not things a normal person says to God. They make the list feel random. There's no gentle grief line ('Hold me', 'Be with me', 'Take care of him').
'Displeased with me' could feel a little heavy-handed to some, but it's fine. 'Clearly at work' sounds like church talk.

results.overall: The quiz is quick and mostly gentle, and 'Someone or something I've lost' let her say what mattered. But the lists lean hard toward enemies and conflict, and they're missing the plain grief words (lonely, sad, 'be with me'), so at three points she had to settle for the nearest option instead of the true one. 'Something hard just ended' and 'I miss You' are traps that could send her the wrong way.

verdict.why: Four months after losing him, the heaviness is the truest thing about my days, and it hasn't lifted, so I'd say "Yes, that's it" to line 1. It is gentle and doesn't try to tell me what kind of trouble I'm in. Psalm 42 does speak to me. Tears day and night, pouring out my soul, deep calling to deep: that is how grief feels. The soul asking itself "why are you downcast?" feels like my own nights, not like someone scolding me. What it doesn't do is name him. Nothing says loss or death, so I'd feel it understood my mood more than what happened to me. Line 2 is wrong for me. I'm not pleading or asking God for anything. I'm missing my husband.
verdict.wouldHurt: "What grieves you is healed" could land a bit fast at four months, like being told the healing is on a schedule. "Put your hope in God, for I will yet praise Him" is fine inside the psalm. Pulled out as the headline, though, it could feel like being told to cheer up. Nothing in it is cruel. It just treats grief over a death as "a weight on your soul". If "Hard words" notes about cursing enemies appeared on a different psalm, those would jar at a time like this. Here they don't.
verdict.theirSituation: She is grieving the recent death of her husband of 50 years. She isn't angry, afraid or asking God for anything. She is sad and misses him, and nothing in the quiz or the result names bereavement.

results.desc: A pastor, 50, whose church board spread a false story about him to the denomination. Two elders he mentored led it.

answers.wanted: Betrayed, or Hurt. Angry fits some days too, but a pastor won't tap Angry easily.
People who turned on me. 'Someone in my life' sounds like one person, and this is a board and two elders.
Both 'Against me' and 'Talking behind my back'. They spread a false story, so both are true and I had to pick one.
People I trusted and trained, who now have power over me. 'Friends', 'People with power over me' and 'A whole group' are all partly true.
It's happening in church, but not because of what I believe. Something like 'It's in my church, but not about belief'.
Being pushed out is a close second.

friction.note: 'Someone in my life' is singular. When a group is against you, it feels like the wrong option, and nothing else fits.

'Against me' and 'Talking behind my back' overlap. Slander is both, and choosing one feels arbitrary. The list also goes from very negative straight to 'Fine', with nothing like 'Mixed: some for me, some against'. Some people stood by him.
There's no word for betrayal or hurt, which is the main feeling when a friend turns on you. 'Heavy' is vague.

Asks for one category when the real answer is a mix: people he mentored, acting as a board, with power over him. It feels like being put in a box. The options are hard to tell apart, so let people pick more than one.

'Because of what I believe' suggests persecution. Church conflict isn't really about belief, so 'Partly' is a guess and 'No' seems to deny the church part. It's confusing for anyone hurt inside a church.
'What they might be planning' and 'Not knowing what they'll do next' read as nearly the same option. Seven options here, where other questions have three to five, feels uneven.

'Why do they get away with it?' and 'You decide who's right.' are specific enough that I could tell they point at particular psalms. They fit this person well, but they feel steered. The rest of the list goes from 'Help.' to 'How great You are.' with no clear order from negative to positive.

results.overall: It's mostly easy and quick, and it clearly understood that he's being wronged by people. But several questions made him choose one option when two were true (against/talking, friends/power/group), and it lacked a plain word for betrayal. So it felt like he was being sorted into a box, not heard.

verdict.why: As this pastor I'd say yes to the first line straight away. "People you thought were your friends are spreading lies about you, others are piling on" is my situation: two elders I mentored started the false story, and the board carried it to the denomination. Psalm 55:13, "it is you, a man like myself, my companion and close friend," hits hard in a good way. It's the verse I'd have picked myself, and seeing it quoted makes the quiz feel like it actually heard me. "Where it turns" at 55:16 gives me something to hold, not just a mirror of the hurt. Two small misses. First, "friends" is softer than what happened: these were men I invested in, so it's closer to betrayal by my own disciples. Second, Athanasius's "idle talk" makes it sound like gossip, when this was a formal accusation that puts my ministry and my name with the denomination at risk. Neither would make me say "Not quite." I never needed lines 2 or 3. Line 2, about a weight that won't lift, is true of me but too vague, and on its own it would have felt like the quiz missed the point.
verdict.wouldHurt: "Idle talk" in Athanasius's advice makes a formal false accusation to the denomination sound like petty gossip. Psalm 55 also has the curse at 55:15 ("let death seize them"). A pastor would handle that, but it's where the quiet "Hard words" note earns its place, because this reader will be tempted by that verse and troubled by it at the same time.
verdict.theirSituation: A pastor betrayed by two elders he mentored, who led the board in sending a false story about him to the denomination, so his reputation and his ministry are at stake.

results.desc: A woman, 29, whose adult sister has cut her off and turned the rest of the family against her.

answers.wanted: Getting worse, it keeps spreading. Each relative who goes quiet makes it worse, so 'getting worse' fits, but it feels more like 'still falling apart' than a trend line.
Hurt, or rejected, or lonely. The list has no word for being hurt by people, so 'Heavy' was the nearest.
My family. 'Someone or something I've lost' fit almost as well, because I've lost my sister and maybe my family. I had to pick between two that were both true.
They've taken her side and pulled away. It's 'Talking behind my back', 'Against me' and 'Far away, or gone' all at once, and I could only tap one.
Why is this happening? or Please fix this / bring them back. 'Why do they get away with it?' is too accusing for my own sister, and 'Help.' was the only neutral option.

friction.note: There is no word for hurt, rejected, betrayed or lonely, and those are the obvious feelings when family cuts you off. 'Heavy' and 'Numb' feel clinical. The nine words mix moods (Calm, Glad) and states (Worn out, Restless) and don't run evenly from bad to good.

'Someone in my life', 'Someone I care about' and 'Someone or something I've lost' overlap for anyone whose problem is a broken relationship. She would stop and wonder which one the quiz means. A family split is all three.

Single choice forces her to pick between 'Against me', 'Talking behind my back' and 'Far away, or gone' when all three are true. 'Against me' sounds dramatic or paranoid. The options jump from hostile to 'A real gift' with no plain 'mixed' or 'some good, some bad', and her friends may be kind while her family isn't.

Most options are strongly flavoured ('Why do they get away with it?', 'You decide who's right.'). They read as boxes aimed at a particular psalm and assume the other side is wicked, which she may not want to say about her sister. Only 'Help.' is neutral. There's nothing like 'Fix this' or 'Bring them back'.

'What they might be planning' and 'Not knowing what they'll do next' sound like a plot or physical danger. That's odd for a family estrangement and a little paranoid. 'That it keeps growing' and 'That it won't stop' are hard to tell apart.
'Is your faith part of it?' comes out of nowhere for a family fight and could feel like a push to spiritualise it. She'd answer No without being sure why it's asked.
'Something hard just ended' and 'Something new just began' are a different kind of answer from worse/same/better. It's one question doing two jobs.
'Displeased with me' stands out as heavier and more guilt-laden than the rest. It's fine as an option, but it's the only one that reads like a confession prompt.

results.overall: Quick and mostly easy, and 'Family, or the people closest to me' plus 'Being pushed out' felt like the quiz really got her. But several screens made her pick one of three answers that were all true, the feelings list had no 'hurt', and the 'say to God' options leaned accusing, so she had to settle for 'Help.'.

verdict.why: Line 1 says exactly what happened to me: my own sister turned on me, and then the rest of the family followed her. "More and more others rising up" is how it felt as each relative went quiet or picked her side. Psalm 3 is David running from his own son, so it is family betrayal and not a stranger enemy, and that is why it lands. The turn at 3:3, "the One who lifts my head", is what I need, because being shut out has left me ashamed as much as hurt. Line 2 was close too, since I have been pushed out. But "on your own" felt like wilderness and loneliness, not betrayal, so I would not have stopped there.
verdict.wouldHurt: "Foes" and "rise up against me" cast my sister as my enemy. I still love her and want her back, so that word stings a little, though the psalm is honest about how it feels. What would hurt more is 3:7, where God strikes enemies on the jaw and breaks the teeth of the wicked. Reading the whole psalm, I would take that as asking God to hurt my sister and my parents. A short note there saying this is David's cry for rescue, not a wish to harm family, would matter a lot for someone in my place. "Hounded" in Athanasius's advice is strong too, but I can live with it.

results.desc: A college student, 20, whose philosophy classmates mock faith. He is starting to doubt, and it scares him.

answers.wanted: Unsure / Confused
Whether any of it is true / What I believe
Mocking what I believe (to my face, not behind my back)
I'm not sure He's there
Are You even real? / Show me You're there.

friction.note: No word for uncertainty or confusion. Doubt is the main thing going on for him and he has to choose between Afraid and Restless.

"God, and where I stand with Him" sounds like guilt or distance from God. It doesn't cover wondering whether God is real, which is his actual question. An option like "Big questions about what I believe" would fit, and it's generic enough to work for other people too.

The classmates mock him openly, in class. That isn't "talking behind my back" and it isn't "against me". "Hard to be around" was the nearest option, but it waters the situation down. Something like "Making fun of me or what I care about" is missing.

"And God, right now, feels…" takes it for granted that God is there. A doubter has no honest option, and it feels like a box for believers only. He needs something like "I'm not sure He's there" or "Hard to tell".

Every option assumes he is talking to Someone he's sure is listening. "Help." was the nearest. "Are You there?" or "Show me" is missing. "Why do they get away with it?" and "You decide who's right." sound oddly specific and courtroom-like to a 20-year-old.

"People mocking God" is the option that describes his situation best, but he never sees it. It only appears if he picks "The way the world is" or "Why do they get away with it?", and he chose neither. His real situation gets missed because of how the questions branch.
This follow-up is skipped when people is "hard", so he never gets a chance to say that being mocked is the hardest part.

results.overall: The quiz was quick and easy to tap through, but it was written for someone who is sure God is there and feels far from Him, not for someone who wonders whether He exists. The questions about God and what he'd say to Him felt like they were for believers only, and the one option that named his situation ("People mocking God") never came up.

verdict.why: Line 1 is not me at all. Line 2, "afraid, and need something to hold on to", is true, since my doubts scare me, so I would tap yes there and never see line 3. Line 3 is the closer fit: people are asking me "Where is your God?" But its opening, "You long for God with everything in you", claims more than a doubter feels able to say right now, so I might have hesitated there anyway. Psalm 118's "What can man do to me?" speaks to the classmates somewhat. What actually scares me, though, is losing my faith, and the psalm treats fear of people, not doubt. Psalm 42, which ends with "Why are you downcast, O my soul? ... Put your hope in God", is the result that would really have landed.
verdict.wouldHurt: Psalm 118 is confident and triumphant ("I will not be afraid"), which could read as "just stop being afraid" to someone whose fear is that his faith is slipping. It says nothing about doubt. Line 3's "with everything in you" overstates the longing, so a doubter might feel he doesn't qualify for the psalm that fits him best. Because line 2 is so generic it comes before line 3 in the order and catches him first.
verdict.theirSituation: He is being mocked for his faith and is frightened by his own growing doubt. What he needs is a psalm that lets a faltering believer argue with his own soul (Psalm 42), not a victory song about fear of other people.

results.desc: A man, 45, laid off after 20 years. Money is tight and he feels useless. Nobody is against him.

answers.wanted: Something like 'Stuck' or 'Not getting better': the layoff isn't new, it's just dragging on and money gets tighter each month
'Useless' or 'Lost' or 'Ashamed'. Heavy is near, but the real feeling is that he's worthless without the job
Something like 'Show me what I'm for.' or 'Don't forget me.' 'Help.' works, but it misses the sense of having lost his purpose

friction.note: There's no word for feeling useless, ashamed or lost. For a laid-off man that's the main feeling, and none of the nine words names it. 'Heavy' and 'Worn out' are the closest, but only just.

Two of the nine options ('Why do they get away with it?' and 'You decide who's right.') assume he has enemies or is in a dispute. For someone whose trouble is circumstance, not people, they look out of place, and they make the list feel written for some other situation. Most real people's prayers are closer to 'Help', 'Please provide' or 'I don't know what to do'.
There's no option about need or provision ('Please provide', 'Give me work'), which is his actual prayer. 'Help.' carries all of it.
'Getting worse' vs 'About the same' is a coin flip when you're stuck in something that's slowly draining you. An option like 'Stuck' or 'Dragging on' would fit many more people.
'Displeased with me' stands out as heavier and more loaded than the rest of the list. Otherwise it's fine; 'Silent' fitted.
The list runs straight from 'Hard to be around' / 'Far away, or gone' to 'Fine'. For him, people are fine but he's pulled away out of shame. There's no option like 'I've been keeping to myself'.

results.overall: Quick and mostly easy. Season, focus and people fitted cleanly, but the quiz never let him say the thing that hurts most, feeling useless, and a couple of the prayer options felt written for someone with enemies rather than someone out of work.

verdict.why: As this man I'd say yes to line 1. Nobody is against me, so a psalm about enemies would feel wrong. What I have is a steady heaviness: the lost job, the bills, feeling useless. Line 1 is general enough to fit without making me explain the layoff. Psalm 42:5 says "Why are you downcast, O my soul?" and then "Put your hope in God, for I will yet praise Him." That is close to the argument I have with myself every morning, and it doesn't ask me to pretend I'm fine. It didn't box me in, and it didn't read me as someone being attacked. What's missing is my actual situation. Nothing about work, being provided for, or feeling useless is named, so the result speaks to my mood but not to my circumstances. "Grinding me down" (Psalm 102) from the fallback list might fit the slow, day-after-day money pressure a little better. Line 2 (pleading) would feel like a stretch. I'm not pleading so much as flattened.
verdict.theirSituation: A long-employed man, newly laid off, short on money and feeling useless. The heaviness comes from his circumstances, not from grief or enemies, and nothing in the result names work, providing or worth.

results.desc: A woman, 33, anxious all the time for no reason she can name. She lies awake at night.

answers.wanted: Honestly it's fine on paper, but I'm not okay inside. Something like 'Fine on the outside, not on the inside'
Anxious, or On edge. 'Afraid' is too strong for a fear with no cause, and 'Restless' sounds like boredom
Everything and nothing, I can't pin it down. 'Nothing in particular' sounds like my mind is empty, and it's the opposite
I don't know. I can't really feel Him either way right now

friction.note: There's no 'Anxious' or 'Worried', and that's the most common feeling people will come with. 'Afraid' suggests a real threat and 'Restless' suggests boredom, so an anxious person has to pick one that is slightly wrong.

'Nothing in particular' is the only choice for worry with no clear cause, but it reads like 'I'm fine, nothing's on my mind'. It could send her to a calm result, which is the opposite of her real state. Something like 'Lots of things, nothing I can name' is needed.
Lying awake and not sleeping, the one concrete sign of her anxiety, has nowhere to go. 'My health' sounds like a diagnosis, not a sleepless night.
The six options only measure how good or bad things are. There's no option for 'things are fine, but I'm not'. That gap is what makes anxiety confusing to her, so the scale feels a bit off.

'Something hard just ended' and 'Something new just began' are a different kind of answer from 'worse / same / better' in the same list. They're fine, but they read as if they're steering toward a specific story.
The list jumps from 'Silent' to 'Near, but quiet'. Neither fits a person who simply can't feel much of anything. A neutral 'Hard to say' would help.
'Why do they get away with it?' and 'You decide who's right' are very specific. They read like the quiz is looking for a particular kind of person, not letting her say what she means.

results.overall: It was quick and mostly gentle, and 'Help.' landed perfectly. But her main problem, anxiety with no cause, had no word of its own anywhere. She had to pick 'Restless' and 'Nothing in particular', which could make the quiz read her as more settled than she is. She'd come away unsure the result really heard her.

verdict.why: She would stop at line 1 and say yes, though with a little hesitation. "Weighing on your soul, and it won't lift" gets the constant, shapeless part of her anxiety, even if "weighing" sounds more like sadness than dread. The psalm gets her better than the line does. "Why the unease within me?" is her question exactly: a soul uneasy for no reason it can name, talking back to itself. Athanasius's advice about smoothing out what is troubled in you also fits someone whose trouble is agitation rather than a loss. Line 2 would feel wrong. She doesn't need to plead for anything in particular, and that is the whole difficulty. The fallback's "It's making me afraid" (Psalm 118) would be her second choice.
verdict.wouldHurt: Nothing wounds her. The only small misread is that "downcast" and "weighing" point toward depression, while she would call herself anxious and restless. The match line never mentions unease, restlessness or sleepless nights, which are her words. If the line said something like "Your soul is uneasy and you can't say why," she would know it was her right away instead of only mostly.
verdict.theirSituation: She is anxious all the time for no reason she can name, and it keeps her awake at night; it feels like a restless unease more than sadness.

There's no word for strong joy. 'Glad' is the top of the scale, and it feels mild next to 'Afraid', 'Heavy' and 'Angry'. Five of the nine words are negative, so the list leans toward the down side.
'Someone coming to faith' is ambiguous. Does 'someone' include me? Someone who was just converted or baptised has no option that clearly speaks about them.
Fits well. It might help to have something like 'Everywhere I look' for people who see Him in everything, but 'Clearly at work' covers it.

verdict.why: Right now I want to thank God for everything, so line 1 is me straight away and I would tap yes. Psalm 103 ("Bless the LORD, O my soul, and do not forget all His kind deeds") is exactly the psalm I would want to pray a month after my baptism. Line 2 comes close, but it describes watching someone else get baptised. I was the one baptised. Oddly, Psalm 32 ("Blessed is he whose transgressions are forgiven") fits my own baptism even better than line 2's wording does. As written, though, it would make me pause and say "not quite, that was me, not someone I watched." The one risk is the fallback. If a joyful person misses both lines, every fallback option is negative (grinding me down, weighing on me, afraid). A happy new believer who lands there would feel the quiz assumed they must be struggling. That is the same pull toward a negative answer the owner complained about.
verdict.theirSituation: A new believer, baptised a month ago, full of joy and wanting to thank God for everything; Psalm 103 fits them well.

I'm holding on to Him / I keep praying and don't know if He's listening
Healing (on its own, without 'a way out')

'My health' made me wonder whether to tap it for his health. It should be clear it means your own body.
'A way out, or healing' is upsetting for a parent of a seriously ill child: 'a way out' can sound like dying. Healing should be its own option. 'Comfort' also sounds like end-of-life care.
The options assume something that was already going on. There is no choice for 'something hard just began', and 'Something new just began' sounds like good news.

Nothing fits someone praying all day without knowing whether they're heard. It's split between 'Silent' (sounds like giving up) and 'Near, but quiet' (sounds too settled). Also, 'Displeased with me' puts the idea of illness as punishment in front of a frightened parent. That may be honest for some people, but it stings.
'Against me' and 'Talking behind my back' feel far from a hospital situation. That's fine, but this is a long list for a scared person on a phone.

'Why do they get away with it?' and 'You decide who's right.' read oddly and feel like they're from someone else's life. 'Help.' fit, but a line like 'Please heal him' / 'Please save them' is what she would really say.

results.overall: Mostly easy and it felt gentle. 'Afraid', 'Help.' and 'Someone I care about' named her situation. It stumbled at the follow-up, where 'A way out, or healing' could read as her son dying, and at the God question, where nothing fits someone who is praying constantly without knowing if she's heard.

verdict.why: As her, I'd say yes to the first line. "You're afraid, and you need something to hold on to" is the truth of my days right now. Line 2 would fit too, since I am praying all the time, but I'd stop at line 1. Line 3's "tired of living afraid" and "help others take heart" is too tidy for where I am. The result mostly holds. "The LORD is my strength and my song" and Athanasius's "whatever in you is afraid is strengthened by hope" are things I could read at a hospital bedside. The weak spot is the opening verse. "What can man do to me?" is about fearing people, and no person is threatening me. My fear is of an illness and of losing my child. So the verse the page points to first answers a fear I don't have, and my real fear goes unnamed. The line also speaks about me, but my whole prayer is for someone else: my son. A psalm framed as "your" fear misses that. And the question, "Which Psalm are you living right now?", feels slightly light next to a child's illness, though the result doesn't make light of it.
verdict.wouldHurt: Leading with 118:6 ("What can man do to me?") treats my fear as fear of enemies. That makes me feel the quiz didn't really hear what I'm afraid of. Psalm 118:17, "I shall not die, but live", is double-edged for a mother whose child is seriously ill. It could comfort her, or it could sting badly if things go badly. Nothing here is cruel, but nothing acknowledges that the fear is for someone I love, not for myself.
verdict.theirSituation: She is terrified her son might not recover and spends the day praying for him. It's a fear and a plea on someone else's behalf, not fear of people who oppose her.

results.desc: A man, 55, whose business rival cheated his way to success while he stayed honest and struggled. He is bitter and envious.

Something like 'Someone who's doing better than me' or 'It's not fair'. What's on his mind is the rival and the unfairness, not work or money as such. 'Someone in my life' feels wrong for a competitor he doesn't really have a relationship with.

Something like 'Someone did me wrong' or 'One person has it out for me / got ahead at my expense'. The people around him day to day are fine. The problem is one rival, and none of these options is about him.

friction.note: The question asks about 'the people around you' in general, so a man with one specific rival has nowhere to put him. 'Against me' and 'Talking behind my back' sound paranoid or like a playground for a 55-year-old businessman. Because I tapped 'Fine', the rival never came up again, and the 'who' follow-up (which has 'One person in particular') never showed.

There's no envy, bitterness or 'it's not fair' among the words. Envy is the heart of this man's situation, but only 'Angry' comes near it. The list jumps from dark words to happy ones with nothing like 'Frustrated' or 'Fed up' in between.

The options mix very different kinds of things: health, God, the world, a loss. A rival cheating him fits two or three of them partly and none of them fully. 'The way the world is' is close too, but it sounds a bit grand.

'Why do they get away with it?' fits him perfectly, but it stands out as so specific that it feels planted, as if the quiz already knew the answer. 'You decide who's right' sounds like church talk. 'How great You are' and 'I miss You' are phrased more devotionally than the rest.
'Displeased with me' is a loaded option. It's fine to offer, but next to 'Clearly at work' the list swings from one extreme to the other.

results.overall: The quiz was quick and mostly easy. It came alive at 'Why do they get away with it?' and 'Bad people doing well', which named his situation exactly. The early questions have no place for envy or for a single rival, so he had to settle for approximate answers ('Angry', 'Work, money', 'Fine'). The result leans almost entirely on two late taps.

verdict.why: He would say yes to the first line. His story fits it closely: someone who cheated is doing well while he stayed honest and struggled. Psalm 73 is the classic psalm for this, and verse 3 ("I envied the arrogant when I saw the prosperity of the wicked") names his envy outright without scolding him. That lets a bitter man admit it, because the psalmist admits it first. The turn at verse 17 gives him somewhere to go (look at where they end up, and go back to God) without asking him to pretend it doesn't hurt. Athanasius's advice, "so that you are not caught out and shaken," fits well. He would feel seen, not boxed in.
verdict.wouldHurt: Nothing that wounds. Two small mismatches. "People who don't care about God" is not how he would describe his rival; he would say the man cheated, not that he was godless. A phrase like "people who cheat or cut corners" would catch him sooner. Also, "it's shaking you" is gentler than what he feels, which is bitter and resentful. He might pause for a second before tapping yes, but he would still tap it.
verdict.theirSituation: A 55-year-old man is bitter and envious because a business rival cheated his way to success while he stayed honest and struggled. He feels wronged by a dishonest person more than he feels shaken by godless people doing well.

results.desc: Denise, 52, Ohio, United Methodist. Her mother has dementia and moved in with her family in the spring; last Sunday her mother didn't know who she was. She is worn out, snaps at her husband over small things, and when she prays it feels like talking to the ceiling.

answers.wanted: Watching someone I love slip away (my mom is still here but I'm losing her; 'Someone I care about' and 'Someone I've lost' both half fit)
Honestly, I've been the hard one to be around (I snap at my husband). Or: I'm the one taking care of everybody
Peace for her, and strength for me to keep caring for her. None of the options include me, the caregiver

friction.note: Every option is about how other people treat me. It never lets me say I'm the problem right now (short-tempered, worn thin). 'Fine' is a lie, 'Hard to be around' sounds like I'm blaming my husband, and 'Far away, or gone' almost fits my mom but seems to mean people who left. The scale jumps from hostile ('Against me', 'Talking behind my back') straight to 'Fine', so there's no everyday middle.
'Someone I care about' and 'Someone or something I've lost' overlap, and anyone watching a parent decline will hesitate between them. There's nowhere for losing someone who is still alive.

'A way out, or healing' stings when there's no cure. 'Someone to help them' misses that I AM the helper, and I'm the one who needs help. All the options look only at the other person, never at the one carrying the load.

Most of the options are fine, but 'Why do they get away with it?' and 'You decide who's right.' feel oddly specific, like they're steering toward enemy psalms. 'I miss You.' nearly fit too. You can only tap one, and the choice between 'Help.' and 'How long?' feels arbitrary. I felt guilty about 'How long?' because it could sound like I'm wishing my mom's life away.

This follow-up never appeared because I didn't pick 'sorry' or 'displeased'. So my real guilt about snapping at my husband never came up. A gentle 'Anything you wish you'd handled better?' asked of everyone would have caught it.

'Something hard just ended' and 'Something new just began' don't fit alongside 'worse / same / better'. They're events, not trends. My mom moving in was 'something new' in the spring, but it's hardly a new start.
There's no 'Sad' or 'Grieving', only 'Heavy', which is close. Mixing 'Restless' and 'Numb' in with the plain moods makes the list feel scattered.

results.overall: For a worn-out caregiver the quiz went quickly and mostly felt kind. But it kept assuming my trouble comes from enemies or from things I did, when really I'm pouring myself out for someone who is slowly slipping away. I never found a spot for 'I'm the one who's hard to live with right now' or 'I need help too', so I finished feeling only partly seen.

verdict.why: As Denise, I'd say yes to the first line. "Worn down," "empty" and "need comfort" describe me this year. "Poor" makes me stop for a second, because we aren't struggling for money, but "life has worn you down" covers the rest. Psalm 102 fits better than I'd expect. "Withered like grass" and "I even forget to eat my bread" is exactly how caregiving days go. The turn, "He will not despise their prayer," answers the ceiling feeling right where it hurts. I wouldn't feel boxed in, because the line names the effect on me and not a situation I have to squeeze into. Line 3 would pull at me a little, since someone I love is in trouble, but I can't pray over my mother in a way she'd know, so it would ring slightly hollow. Line 2 is too generic to catch me. The fallback option "It's grinding me down" would also land me on Psalm 102, so I end up in the right place either way. What's missing is the part that makes this different from ordinary exhaustion: grieving someone who is still alive, and the guilt about snapping at my husband. The result helps, but it doesn't name those.
verdict.wouldHurt: "Poor" can read as being about money and feels a little off for a tired, middle-class caregiver. "Worn down, drained" would read better. Nothing in the psalm itself would wound me, though the later verses about God having "lifted me up and cast me away" could sting on a bad day.
verdict.theirSituation: She is caring for her mother with dementia and grieving a mother who no longer knows her. She is exhausted, short-tempered with her husband and guilty about it, and she feels her prayers go nowhere.

results.desc: Kwame, 34, Accra, Ghana, Pentecostal. A coworker told their manager that Kwame had been taking money from petty cash, and there is now an investigation even though he did nothing. He is angry and scared of losing the job, and his wife keeps telling him to pray while he mostly lies awake rehearsing what he'll say.

answers.wanted: Angry and afraid both; I'd want to tap two words, or 'Angry and scared'
Being accused of something I didn't do at work. It's the coworker AND the job at once, so 'Someone in my life' and 'Work, money or what's next' both half-fit
'One person has turned on me'. It's one coworker, not 'the people around me'; my wife is on my side, so the plural question doesn't fit
Something like 'I haven't really been talking to Him': the distance is on my side, not His
'Clear my name' / 'Defend me'. 'You decide who's right' sounds like a court case with me possibly in the wrong, and I know I'm innocent
'Being accused of something I didn't do' / 'That people might believe it'. The lie and losing the job are what hurt, more than their words as such

friction.note: Only one word allowed, and anger and fear arrive together for someone falsely accused. Forcing a choice felt arbitrary.

'Someone in my life' is so vague it almost doesn't read as 'someone causing me trouble'. It sounds like romance or family. No option covers 'a problem at work involving a person', so the obvious answer is split across two options.

'The people around you' assumes a group. When one person is the problem and your family is supportive, none of the options is right: 'Against me' and 'Talking behind my back' overstate it, and 'Fine' or 'Kind to me' ignore it. Something like 'Mostly fine, but one person...' is missing.
The options mix different kinds of answers (hostile, distant, gone, kind, a gift), so the list reads as scattered rather than a scale.

'Displeased with me' stands out as a pointed, guilt-leaning option. Most of the options also describe God's side; there is nothing for 'I've been too upset to pray', which is the honest answer for a lot of people.

'You decide who's right' is an odd, stiff phrase. An innocent person wants to be defended or cleared, not judged. 'Why do they get away with it?' also nearly fits, which makes the choice feel like a guess. Nine options is a lot to scan on a phone.

'What they might be planning' and 'Feeling trapped' sound paranoid or dramatic. The plain answer, 'being lied about', isn't there. The seven options feel like variations on one theme, as if the quiz is steering toward a specific psalm.
Some options ('Being pushed out', 'That it keeps growing') are oddly specific and made me feel I was being sorted into a pre-made box.

results.overall: It was quick and mostly easy to get through, and I could tell early on that it had noticed people were against me. But almost every question made me split one situation, a false accusation at work, across two half-fitting options. The quiz never just let me say 'someone lied about me and I'm scared for my job', so I finished feeling approximated rather than understood.

verdict.why: As Kwame, I'd feel let down, and a bit misread. My situation is one of the oldest in the Psalter: someone lied about me, and now I'm under investigation. Athanasius's letter covers being slandered, plotted against and falsely accused (he points readers to psalms like 7, 27 and 35 for that). So when the quiz tells me "his letter doesn't name what you're going through", my answers have been lost somewhere, not the letter. The fallback gets me halfway there. "It's making me afraid" (Psalm 118: "The LORD is on my side; I will not fear: what can man do unto me?") would actually land with me, and I'd tap it. But it only covers my fear. It misses the anger and the sense of injustice, and those are what keep me awake rehearsing my defence. The other two options ("grinding me down", "weighing on me") read as depression or long illness, not a sudden false accusation. What I'd need is a line like "Someone is telling lies about me" or "I'm being blamed for something I didn't do." That's broad enough for lots of people (office politics, family rumours, a church falling-out) without boxing anyone in. It's also exactly the kind of generic, wider-net answer the owner is asking for.
verdict.wouldHurt: Being told the letter "doesn't name" false accusation feels dismissive, because it does name it. It implies my trouble is too unusual for Scripture's own prayer book, when being falsely accused is one of the psalms' central themes.
verdict.theirSituation: A coworker falsely accused him of taking petty cash, and he now faces an investigation. He is angry at the injustice, afraid of losing his job, and lies awake rehearsing his defence instead of praying.

results.desc: Rachel, 38, Manchester, UK, Church of England. Their third round of IVF failed last month, and two friends have announced pregnancies since. She has stopped going to the family service and isn't sure God is listening, though she hasn't said that out loud to anyone.

answers.wanted: Something hard just happened and it's still raw (the IVF failed a month ago and hasn't 'ended' in any sense)
Something I've been longing for and can't have (a baby I never had, so 'lost' feels slightly off)
Just 'Why?' or 'Are You even listening?'
Friends, but they haven't done anything wrong; it's their good news that's hard

friction.note: 'Hard to be around' is the only option that fits, but it then leads to follow-ups written as if people are hostile. Her friends are kind; their happy news is what hurts. She'd feel guilty being lumped in with 'against me'. An option like 'Happy in ways that hurt to watch' or 'I've been keeping away' would fit better.
'Is your faith part of it?' reads like a persecution question. For someone whose pain is envy and grief, it doesn't make sense and feels like the quiz misread her.
'Who are they, mostly?' sounds like it's asking who the enemy is. Uncomfortable when nobody has done anything wrong.
The only 'why' option is 'Why do they get away with it?', which accuses someone. Many hurting people just want to ask 'Why?' or 'Are You listening?' 'How long?' is close but assumes this ends.
'Someone or something I've lost' only half fits a hope that never came true (failed IVF, miscarriage, singleness). A broader 'Something I long for and don't have' would reach more people.
Nothing fits 'something hard just happened and it's still raw'. 'Something hard just ended' could be misread as the IVF process ending, which would send her down the wrong path.
Fine, but she has doubts she hasn't said out loud. 'Silent' fits; an option like 'I'm not sure He's listening' would be more honest for doubters.

results.overall: The first three and the question about God felt gentle and accurate, but once she tapped 'Hard to be around' the quiz moved into questions about enemies and persecution that don't fit someone grieving a hope while her friends celebrate. She'd feel a bit misunderstood, maybe a bit guilty, and would likely finish wondering whether the psalm she got is really about her.

verdict.why: As Rachel, I would tap "Yes, that's it" on this line. It doesn't name IVF, and I'm glad it doesn't, because I haven't said any of this out loud, and a quiz that guessed "infertility" would feel invasive. "Weighing on your soul, and it won't lift" is general enough that I can say yes to it privately, and it's true. It has been a month and the weight hasn't moved. Psalm 42 turns out to be almost uncannily right once I read it in full. Verse 3 has tears as food "while they say to me all day long, Where is your God?" That's the question I haven't dared say to anyone. Verse 4 remembers going "with the multitude to the house of God" with gladness, which is exactly what I've stopped doing with the family service. The psalm argues with itself instead of resolving neatly, and that fits where I am. The quiz earns this result without boxing me in, but the card undersells it. It only shows the two "put your hope in God" refrains, and those read as instructions to cheer up. The verses that would make me feel seen, 3 and 4, aren't quoted on the card.
verdict.wouldHurt: For someone who isn't sure God is listening, the card's framing leans too fast toward the answer. Both verses shown are the "Put your hope in God, for I will yet praise Him" refrain. Athanasius's line that "what grieves you is healed" also reads like a promise of quick repair, when the wound is fresh and friends keep announcing pregnancies. It could feel like being told to get over it. The fix is to show the tears or "Where is your God?" verse (42:3) or the house-of-God verse (42:4) as the opening, and let the hope refrain be where it turns. The psalm itself doesn't wound. The selection of verses on the card risks it.
verdict.theirSituation: Rachel is grieving a third failed round of IVF while friends announce pregnancies. She has quietly withdrawn from church and privately doubts God is listening, so what she needs is permission to lament before anyone points her to hope.

results.desc: Tom, 44, Houston, Texas, non-denominational church. He started drinking again after fourteen months sober and hasn't told his sponsor or his wife. He feels deeply ashamed and half believes God has run out of patience with him.

answers.wanted: Ashamed
They don't know what's really going on with me / I'm hiding something from them
Tired of me, like He's run out of patience
I'm sorry, and help: both at once, like 'I did it again, please don't give up on me'

friction.note: No word for shame or guilt. 'Heavy' is the closest, but the thing he actually feels (ashamed) is missing, and for someone who has slipped it's the obvious word.

All options describe how people treat me. When the problem is that I'm hiding from them (spouse, sponsor), none fit. 'Fine' feels like a lie; an option like 'They don't know what I'm going through' is needed.

'Displeased with me' is close but a bit formal. What he fears is that God is done with him or out of patience with him. Also, the list jumps from 'Silent' to 'Near, but quiet', which are hard to tell apart.

Only one pick. 'I'm sorry' and 'Help' both fit, and choosing one feels like dropping half of it. 'Why do they get away with it?' and 'You decide who's right' are very specific and read strangely next to the rest.

'Something I did' and 'Something I keep going back to' overlap for a relapse. 'A sense that God is warning me' sounds preachy and a bit leading. The habit option fits well without naming the addiction, which is good.
'Something hard just ended' and 'Something new just began' are events, not comparisons, so they don't answer 'compared with a few months ago'. They get mixed in with worse, same and better.
'Someone in my life' and 'Someone I care about' are hard to tell apart on a quick read.

results.overall: It moved quickly and the habit follow-up felt surprisingly on target without naming drinking, but the missing 'ashamed' word and a people question that only covers others being against you made him feel slightly unseen. He had to pick near-misses at the moments that mattered most.

verdict.why: As Tom, the first line is exactly where I am: I did wrong by drinking again, I know it, I'm ashamed, and part of me wants to come back. It doesn't name drinking or relapse. I'm glad it doesn't, because a quiz that said "relapse" to me would feel like it had caught me out. But I'd recognise myself in it straight away. Psalm 51 answers the fear I'm quietest about, that God has run out of patience with me. It opens by appealing to His "loving devotion" and "great compassion", and it turns on "wash me, and I will be whiter than snow". That tells me coming back is still open, and it doesn't pretend nothing happened. Athanasius's note, "you are turning back, and you are asking for mercy", treats me as someone already on the way home. For a man who half believes the door has shut, that matters. The result is also David's psalm after his own great fall, and knowing that helps: a man of God fell badly too. Line 2 ("a warning from God") would have scared me more, and line 3 is too vague. The quiz put the right line first. One gap: I'm hiding this from my wife and my sponsor. Nothing in the line or the advice touches the secrecy, which is half of what is eating me. Psalm 32 ("when I kept silent, my bones wasted away") would speak to that directly. It could work as a second psalm or a quiet "if you haven't told anyone yet" note under this result.
verdict.wouldHurt: Nothing wounds. "You've done wrong, you know it" is blunt, but it's fair, and I'd rather hear it straight. It would only land badly if the result page stopped at confession and never showed the mercy. The "whiter than snow" turn stops that from happening, so keep it visible above the fold.
verdict.theirSituation: A man who has relapsed after fourteen months sober, is hiding it from his wife and sponsor, and fears God has run out of patience with him.

results.desc: Maria, 29, Mexico City, Catholic. Her husband left her for someone at his work, and the divorce is being finalised while she and her four-year-old live with her parents. She still goes to Mass but usually cries through it, and she feels embarrassed in front of people who were at the wedding.

answers.wanted: Something is ending right now, and it's still happening (the divorce is being finalised)
Hurt, or ashamed. Heavy is near, but the embarrassment is a big part of it
Someone who betrayed me / my marriage ending. I was torn between 'Someone in my life' and 'Someone or something I've lost'
Mixed: my family is kind, but one person hurt me badly and I feel judged by others. There's no way to say some are kind and some aren't
Near, but I can't feel Him. I still go to Mass, but I just cry
Why did this happen to me? 'Why do they get away with it?' is about other people in general, not one person who left

friction.note: You can only give one answer for everyone. Her parents are kind, her husband betrayed her, and the wedding guests make her feel ashamed. She has to pick 'Kind to me', and then the betrayal never comes up in any follow-up.

There is no 'one person hurt me' option on the main question. 'One person in particular' only appears if she has already said people are against her, but her family isn't. So the most important fact about her life has nowhere to go.
'Someone in my life' and 'Someone or something I've lost' overlap for a spouse who left. 'Someone in my life' is vague enough to mean anything.
Nothing covers 'something is ending and it's still going on'. 'Something hard just ended' sounds like relief, and she feels none.
There are no relational feelings like hurt, ashamed, lonely or betrayed. Most of the list is about energy (tired, restless, calm), so the social pain she feels most has no word.

'Why do they get away with it?' assumes a group of wrongdoers, and 'You decide who's right.' sounds legalistic and odd to say to God. Neither fits a personal betrayal. A plain 'Why?' or 'Why me?' is missing.
'Displeased with me' pushes toward guilt, and 'Clearly at work' toward piety. What's missing is the middle ground a churchgoer who is hurting would pick: 'I know He's there but I can't feel Him.'
'How long?' and 'Help.' are close, and she could have tapped either. Having both makes her second-guess herself on a phone.

results.overall: The quiz was quick and felt gentle, but none of the answers let Maria say that someone she loved betrayed her and that she feels ashamed in front of others. She finished feeling the quiz had missed the main thing about her life. Most of her answers were 'close enough' rather than right, and none of the follow-up questions came up to catch what had been missed.

verdict.why: As Maria I would say yes to the first line. The heaviness that won't lift is exactly how I live right now: I cry through Mass every week and it doesn't ease. The line is gentle and doesn't ask me to explain the divorce, which I like. Psalm 42 fits better than the two verses shown suggest. The body of the psalm has "my tears have been my food day and night" and a memory of going to the house of God with the crowd, and that is me crying at Mass in front of people who were at my wedding. Once I read the whole psalm I would feel truly seen. The "Why are you downcast, O my soul?" refrain is something I could say to myself during Mass. Athanasius saying that what grieves you is healed gives me hope without telling me to cheer up. Line 2, pleading with God, is also partly true, but it would feel generic. The result does miss one thing: my real wound is being betrayed and left, and the humiliation of it. Nothing on this screen names that, so I feel seen in my sadness but not in my story. If the preview showed 42:3 (the tears verse) instead of repeating the refrain twice, I would recognise myself right away.
verdict.wouldHurt: Nothing wounds. A small miss: the two excerpts shown are almost the same refrain twice, so on first glance the result reads as generic sadness. The verses that would really reach her (42:3, tears day and night and "Where is your God?"; 42:4, going to the house of God with the crowd) are not in the preview.
verdict.theirSituation: Her husband betrayed and left her, and she is grieving the marriage and ashamed in front of the people she sees at Mass. The heaviness is real, but its source is abandonment, and the result doesn't name that.

answers.wanted: Quieter, lonelier than at first (the calls have stopped). It isn't worse or better, it's emptier.
Lonely
They were there at first, but they've gone back to their own lives
I talk to Him, but I don't know if He's listening
Are You there? / Stay with me. / Look after him for me.

friction.note: There's no 'Lonely' or 'Sad'. For a widow those are the obvious words. 'Heavy' is near, but it feels like a stand-in.
'Something hard just ended' could be read as her husband's death. That's jarring: a death isn't a hard thing that 'ended'. Nothing fits a slow fade, where the support drained away after the funeral.

Nothing covers lonely prayer ('Are You listening?', 'Stay with me'). 'I miss You.' could be misread as missing her husband. 'Help.' is the only fallback, and it's too generic.
'Silent' and 'Near, but quiet' are hard to tell apart for someone who talks to God and doesn't know if He hears. A plain 'I'm not sure He's listening' would fit many grieving people.
