There was no 'lonely' word, no follow-up after she named a loss, and the last question was built for people with enemies or great joy. By the end she felt she had been steered away from what she actually said, not into it.

verdict.why: Four months after her husband died, the evenings are silent and the calls have stopped. "Something is weighing on your soul, and it won't lift" is true of her, so she would tap yes. It is not a complete description, though. It describes heaviness. It does not name the loss or the loneliness, so she feels partly seen rather than fully known. Psalm 42 turns out to fit her better than the line suggests. The psalm itself says "my tears have been my food day and night" and "Where is your God?", and 42:9 asks "Why have You forgotten me?". That is very close to her talking to God in the evenings without knowing whether anyone answers. Because the psalm is printed in full, she would find those verses, and they would move her. The line underneath, "Put your hope in God, for I will yet praise Him", gives her hope without dismissing her grief. Line 2, pleading with God, would not have fit her. She is not asking God for something. She is talking to Him the way she talked to her husband. The fallback would also have landed, through "It's weighing on me, and it won't lift".
verdict.wouldHurt: Nothing wounds her. The only gap is that neither the line nor Athanasius's advice mentions grief, being alone, or feeling that God is silent. She has to find those herself in the psalm's verses. The snippets the quiz shows her, 42:5 and 42:11, are the "hope in God" verses, so on that screen the result can read like a general "cheer up, soul" word. The verses that would really reach her, 42:3 and 42:9, are not shown there.
verdict.theirSituation: She is a recently widowed woman whose support has faded away, and she is lonely in the evenings, talking to God as she once talked to her husband and unsure anyone is listening.

results.desc: Daniel, 19, Nairobi, Kenya, Anglican. He didn't get the grades for the university course his parents had been counting on, and his cousins all did. He feels like a disappointment and doubts God pays attention to something as small as exam results.

answers.wanted: Something bad just happened (the results just came out; it isn't a slow slide, it's one blow)
Ashamed / Like I've let people down
School, exams or my future ("work, money" doesn't sound like a 19-year-old student; nearly tapped "Something I've done" because failing feels like his fault)
Disappointed in me (they aren't against him or gossiping; they're let down, and he's being compared to his cousins)
Not bothered with something this small / Like He doesn't care about this
Do You even care about this? / Why did this happen to me?

friction.note: It mixes a direction (worse, same, better) with events (something ended, something began). There's nothing for 'something bad just happened', and that is the most common reason someone has a hard stretch.
There's no word for shame or letting people down, and that's the main feeling for anyone who has failed at something. 'Heavy' is vague. There are nine words, which is a lot to read on a phone.
'Work, money or what's next' reads as an adult's worries. Students would want 'school or exams'. 'Something I've done' pulls toward guilt when he only failed exams.

'Against me' and 'Talking behind my back' are dramatic, and three of the seven options are hostile. There's no middle ground like 'Disappointed in me' or 'Comparing me to others'. It feels like a box meant for people with enemies.
'Is your faith part of it?' seems random when the problem is family disappointment over exams. It's a little confusing to be asked it.
It skips the most common doubt, 'Does He even care about small things like this?' 'Displeased with me' and 'Clearly at work' sound like church talk.

'Why do they get away with it?' and 'You decide who's right' make no sense unless you have enemies, and they feel oddly specific. There is no plain 'Why?' or 'Do You care?' The nine options are unevenly spread: about three negative-general, three enemy-specific and two praise.
'People with power over me' fits parents too. Family and authority overlap for a young person.

results.overall: Quick and mostly easy to tap, but Daniel's real situation (letting his family down, being compared to his cousins, wondering whether God cares about something this small) never quite showed up. He kept settling for the nearest option, and several questions seemed built for someone with enemies or a big sin, not an ordinary setback.

verdict.why: As Daniel I would stop at line 1. Missing the grades my parents were counting on, while my cousins all made it, sits on me every day, so "weighing on your soul, and it won't lift" is close enough to say yes. Psalm 42 suits me well. Its refrain talks to a soul that is downcast, and the psalm goes on to ask God "Why have You forgotten me?", which is my real fear that He doesn't notice something as small as exam results. Athanasius's advice is gentle and has no blame in it. Line 2 would feel wrong. I am not pleading with God. I am half-sure He isn't listening, so I would never pick it. What the line does not catch is shame. My feeling comes from letting my family down and being compared with my cousins, not a vague heaviness. So I feel mostly seen, not exactly seen.
verdict.wouldHurt: Nothing wounds me. "It won't lift" is a little strong for a disappointment I am still living through, and the result never says whether God cares about small things. The psalm answers that only if I read as far as "Why have You forgotten me?" and the hope after it.
verdict.theirSituation: A young Anglican in Nairobi who missed the grades his family expected, feels ashamed next to his cousins, and doubts God notices something so small.

results.desc: Grace, 47, Seoul, South Korea, Presbyterian. Her lupus has flared badly for two months and she has had to cut back her hours at work. She is tired of being tired and a little tired of people telling her they are praying for her healing.

answers.wanted: It comes and goes. It's a chronic illness in a flare, so it's worse than six months ago but not getting steadily worse or better. 'Worse lately, but it's a long thing' would fit.
Kind, but they don't really get it. They mean well, and it still wears me out. The only other choice was 'Hard to be around', and that's too harsh for people who are trying.
I trust Him, but He hasn't answered about this. 'Silent' sounds a bit colder than she feels, and 'Near, but quiet' sounds a bit warmer.

friction.note: The choices assume life moves one way: worse, same or better. Chronic illness goes in cycles of flares and quieter spells, and none of the five fits that. 'Something new just began' could even be misread as the flare itself.

The scale jumps from 'Hard to be around' straight to 'Fine' and 'Kind to me'. There's nothing for 'kind, but draining' or 'they mean well, but it doesn't help', which is exactly what a sick person gets from people saying they're praying for her healing. The negative end has four sharp options (against, talking, hard, gone) and the middle is thin, so the list feels lopsided.
'Displeased with me' could hurt someone who is ill, because it hints that the illness might be a punishment. It's fine as one option among several, but this person would wince at it.

'Why do they get away with it?' and 'You decide who's right.' read as oddly specific, as if they were written for a psalm about enemies. They look out of place next to plain lines like 'Help.' She would skip past them without much thought, but they show what the quiz is steering toward.

'My health' fits well, but no follow-up comes after it, while the people, sin and world answers each get a follow-up. After naming the main thing in her life, it feels a little brushed past: nothing asks whether it's pain, exhaustion, fear or losing her work.
The list is good. 'Worn out' is spot on. It could use a word for 'fed up' or 'frustrated', which sits between 'Worn out' and 'Angry'.

results.overall: Quick and mostly easy. Three answers fit her exactly (hard season, worn out, my health), and 'How long?' felt like it was written for her. The people and God questions made her choose between answers a little too cold or a little too warm. Nothing let her say that the people around her mean well but still wear her out, and that's a big part of how she feels right now.

verdict.why: As Grace I would tap "Yes, that's it" on the first line. "Worn down until you feel empty and listless, and you need comfort" is exactly what "tired of being tired" feels like after two months of a flare. It asks nothing of me: it doesn't want me to be hopeful, and it doesn't promise healing, which is a relief because I'm weary of people doing that. Psalm 102 fits better than the summary line lets on. "Withered like grass", forgetting to eat, and later "He weakened my strength in the way" read like a lupus flare. The turn at 102:17, that He does not despise the prayer of the destitute, comforts me without telling me I'll be cured. I feel seen, not boxed in. Two things keep it from being exact. First, the line says "life" has worn me down, when it is my own body, and nothing names illness. Second, "poor" sounds odd to me, though cutting my hours makes it partly true. The illness wording is still general enough to cover me, which is what the owner wants.
verdict.wouldHurt: "Poor" in the summary line could read as being about money and feel slightly off. Psalm 102:23-24 ("He shortened my days... take me not away in the midst of my days") could land hard for someone with a serious chronic illness. That is honest lament, so keep it, but don't frame it cheerfully. If the 988 crisis line shows on this path, it is a US number and useless to someone in Seoul. Crisis help should be local or international.
verdict.theirSituation: A long lupus flare has worn her body out and forced her to cut her work hours, and she wants comfort that doesn't depend on being told she'll be healed.

results.desc: Mark, 57, Atlanta, Georgia, Baptist. He was laid off in June and the credit card debt is now about forty thousand dollars; nobody at church knows. He wakes at 3 a.m. doing sums in his head and feels like he failed his family.

answers.wanted: Ashamed, or like a failure. Also 'Stressed' or 'Anxious': 'Afraid' is close, but grown men do not call it that.
They don't know what I'm going through / I'm keeping it from them
Somewhere between silent and far. Maybe 'I haven't really been talking to Him'

friction.note: No word for shame, failure or worry. The main thing he feels is that he let his family down, and nothing on the list names it. 'Afraid' sounds too dramatic for how a 57-year-old man would describe himself, and 'Stressed' or 'Worried' is missing.

'Something I've done' pulls at him because he blames himself for the debt. It isn't clear whether it means sin or a mistake, so he wavers between it and 'Work, money or what's next'. The quiz only ever learns one of the two.
Every option describes how people are treating him. The situation he is in, keeping it from them, has no option, so 'Fine' feels like a lie he is telling the quiz too.
'A real gift' reads oddly as a description of people being around you.
'Why do they get away with it?' and 'You decide who's right.' assume an enemy he doesn't have, so they read as oddly specific filler next to the others.
'I'm sorry' is also near for him (sorry to his family more than to God). He can't show both help and guilt.
His path asks no follow-ups at all, so the quiz never learns this is about money shame and secrecy rather than general hardship. It may feel too thin to earn a specific psalm.

results.overall: It was quick and mostly easy, and the money option fit him exactly. But the feelings and people questions had no room for shame and secrecy, which are the heart of what he's carrying. He'd finish unsure the result was really about him.

verdict.why: As Mark, I would tap yes on line 1 without thinking twice. "Weighing on your soul, and it won't lift" is exactly what the 3 a.m. sums feel like: it doesn't let up and it doesn't go away in the morning. It doesn't name money or shame, and that actually helps, because I wouldn't want a website to spell out my debt, and the line is general enough that I can put my situation into it. Psalm 42 fits better than I'd expect: the soul is cast down, "tears have been my food", "deep calls to deep", and then the refrain where he talks to himself, "Put your hope in God." That's the argument I have with myself at night. Athanasius's advice, to speak to your own soul, gives me something to actually do at 3 a.m. Line 2, "plead with God and want words to pray with", would also be true, but it sounds generic and churchy, and it isn't what I'd notice first. The fallback lines were fine too; "It's grinding me down" (102) would have worked.
verdict.wouldHurt: Nothing wounds. One mild sting: Psalm 42 grieves being cut off from going with the crowd to God's house, and Mark is hiding his trouble from his own church, so that verse could land as quiet guilt. It could also read as an invitation to tell someone, which might be good for him. The result names nothing about shame before his family or the fear about providing for them, so the "failed my family" part goes unaddressed. That's fine as long as the line never claims to name it.
verdict.theirSituation: A laid-off 57-year-old in secret debt who feels like he failed his family. The ongoing heaviness is what he'd recognise first; the shame and the money itself stay unspoken.

results.desc: Elena, 24, Bucharest, Romania, Orthodox. Her boyfriend of three years ended it, saying she was too religious and he couldn't see a future. She keeps looking at old photos, has skipped the Liturgy for three weeks, and doesn't quite know how she feels about God right now.

answers.wanted: Something ended that I didn't want to end. "Something hard just ended" sounds like relief, so it doesn't fit a breakup, and "Getting worse" isn't quite right either, because it hit all at once and now I'm stuck.
Sad, or heartbroken. There's no plain "sad", and "heavy" is the nearest.
The person who mattered most left me. Everyone else is fine. "Far away, or gone" sounds like everyone, not one person.
I'm not sure. I'm the one who's been keeping my distance. "Far away" makes it sound like God moved, when I'm the one who stopped going to Liturgy.
Why? Was it worth it? A plain "Why?" about my own life, not "Why do they get away with it?", which is about bad people and doesn't fit me.

friction.note: "Something hard just ended" sounds like good news, as if a hard time is over. When a relationship ends, the ending is the hard thing, so these options don't cover it. There's no neutral "Something ended" option.
No plain "Sad" or "Lonely", which are the most common words after a breakup. The options skew to dramatic words (Afraid, Angry, Numb), with only three positive ones and nothing gently in between.

The options mix how people treat me (Against me, Talking behind my back) with how far away they are (Far away, or gone). If one person left and everyone else is fine, it's hard to know whether to tap Gone or Fine.

Every negative option puts the distance on God (far, displeased, silent). Nothing covers "I've been avoiding Him" or "I don't know how I feel". For someone who skipped church, it feels like being asked to blame Him.

This is the least even question. Several options are very specific ("Why do they get away with it?", "You decide who's right.") and read like they were written for particular psalms. There's no general "Why?" and no "I don't know what to say". "How great You are" feels out of place for someone who's hurting.
"You decide who's right" is confusing out of context. A breakup has no villain in court.

results.overall: For a heartbroken Orthodox woman, the quiz was quick and felt gentle, but none of the questions let her say \"someone left me\" plainly. She kept picking near-misses (heavy, gone, far), and each one pushed her story toward enemies or blaming God rather than grief and her own drifting away.

verdict.why: As Elena, I'd say yes to line 1. It's broad enough to be true without naming the breakup or putting a label on my faith, which I'd resent right now. It's a quiet heaviness that won't lift, and that is how I feel. Psalm 42 fits better than the card lets on. The full psalm has "my tears have been my food," people asking "where is your God?" (my boyfriend basically said my God was the problem), and a memory of going up to the house of God with the crowd, when I've missed the Liturgy for three weeks. The psalm also talks to its own downcast soul without forcing an answer, which suits someone who doesn't know how she feels about God. The card shows only the "put your hope in God" lines, so it reads as more generic and more like advice than the psalm really is. Line 2 would feel like a test I'm failing right now, and I'd skip it.
verdict.wouldHurt: Nothing wounds, but three things could be better. First, Athanasius's advice starts with "Sing the Psalms," which is a bit of an order to someone who has stopped going to church. It works better if it reads as an invitation. Second, as an Orthodox woman I know this as Psalm 41 in the Septuagint/Slavonic/Romanian numbering, and so did Athanasius. If the card says only "Psalm 42," I'll wonder if it's the same psalm. Show both numbers for Orthodox and Catholic readers. Third, the card's excerpt leaves out the verses that would really land for me: the tears, "where is your God?", and the memory of going to the house of God. Put one of those on the card so I feel seen, not just advised.
verdict.theirSituation: She's a young Orthodox woman grieving a breakup in which her faith was the stated reason. She's drifted from church and feels numb and unsure toward God, so it's heartbreak mixed with spiritual distance.

results.desc: James, 66, Glasgow, Scotland, Church of Scotland. His younger brother has cut him off over their father's estate and has been telling the rest of the family things about him that aren't true. He is bitter about it, knows he's meant to forgive, and doesn't want to yet.

answers.wanted: Dragging on and souring: it's not new, but the lies are spreading further through the family
Bitter, or hurt. Angry is too hot for a slow grudge he's nursing
One person has turned on me; the rest are mostly fine but hearing lies about me
Waiting on me: I know what He's asking and I'm not ready to do it
Both 'Family' and 'One person in particular': my brother. Would have liked to tap both

friction.note: No word for bitter, hurt or resentful. A grudge isn't 'Angry'; a Scots man of 66 would hesitate over calling himself angry and has nothing gentler to tap.

'The people around you' is plural, but his trouble is one brother. The rest of the family are just hearing things, so 'Against me' and 'Talking behind my back' both overstate it, and 'Fine' doesn't fit either. It pushes one person's feud into looking like a crowd.

Every option is about how God feels toward him. Nothing covers 'I know what He wants from me (forgive) and I don't want to yet', which is the heart of his situation. 'Displeased with me' is close but sounds like guilt over a sin, not a nudge he's resisting.

No honest option for 'Not yet' or 'Don't ask me to forgive him'. 'What do You want from me?' sounds exasperated rather than reluctant. He took 'You decide who's right', but it's missing the fact that he knows he should forgive.
'Family' and 'One person in particular' overlap for him, and he can only pick one. Letting him pick both, or adding 'Someone in my own family', would fix it.

Asking 'Is your faith part of it?' about a quarrel over an estate feels odd and a bit leading, as if the quiz expects persecution. 'No' is easy enough, but it reads like the quiz has a box ready for him.

'What they might be planning' and 'Feeling trapped' sound dramatic for a family estate feud, like options written for a psalm's enemies rather than real life. 'What they're saying about me' fits well.
'Something hard just ended' and 'Something new just began' sit oddly beside the worse/same/better options. They answer a different question, so the list doesn't read as one scale.

results.overall: He got through it quickly, and the questions about people and slander fit him well. But the quiz has nowhere to say what actually matters: he's bitter, knows he should forgive, and won't yet. The feeling, God and "say one thing" questions all nudged him toward something angrier, more wronged or more guilty than he really is.

verdict.why: The first half lands straight away. "Your own people have turned on you" is my brother, and the story of Absalom rising against his own father is a family betrayal, so Psalm 3 feels like it was picked for me and not a stretch. The second half is a bit big for what I'm living. My brother's lies have turned a cousin or two, not "more and more" people "rising up", and "foes" is a hard word for my own family. I'd still tap "Yes, that's it", because nothing further down the list would be closer. The psalm speaks to the hurt and the feeling of being lied about ("the One who lifts my head" means something when your name is being dragged through the family). But it only sees me as the wronged party. It says nothing about the bitterness I'm carrying or the forgiveness I'm putting off, which is the part actually eating at me. So I'd feel comforted, maybe a wee bit let off the hook, and not fully seen.
verdict.wouldHurt: Nothing wounding. The only jar is the dramatic scale: "foes increased" and "many rise up against me" overstate a family estate row where a few relatives have been told lies. It could read as flattering my grievance rather than naming my struggle to forgive.
verdict.theirSituation: His brother has turned on him over their father's estate and has told a few relatives lies about him. He is hurt and bitter, and he is holding back forgiveness he knows he owes.

results.desc: Sofia, 15, São Paulo, Brazil, evangelical. A group of girls at school have started a group chat that mocks her, and screenshots keep getting passed around. Her parents don't know; she prays at night for it to stop and feels anxious every morning on the bus.
