Anxious, or Nervous. 'Afraid' sounds too strong for a knot in my stomach on the bus
Some people at school, or people my age. 'Someone in my life' sounds like one person, and this is a group
Making fun of me. They aren't only talking behind my back, they post it and pass it around
Something like 'I pray but nothing changes'. I don't really feel He's far away, I just don't see an answer yet
A group of people my age, or people at school. 'A whole group of people' sounds like everyone, or like a crowd

friction.note: 'Someone in my life' is singular, but what hurts a lot of teens is a group. 'Work, money or what's next' is for adults; a 15-year-old would want 'School' on the list.

'Talking behind my back' does not fit mocking that happens openly in a group chat. 'Against me' sounds too dramatic for a teen to tap. Neither one is the plain 'People are mean to me' or 'Making fun of me'.
There is no 'Anxious' or 'Worried', and that is the most common feeling for young people. 'Afraid' and 'Heavy' are a near miss, so she has to guess between them.
'Silent' and 'Near, but quiet' are hard to tell apart for a teen. 'Displeased with me' feels heavy, like it could make a scared kid feel worse just from reading it.

'You decide who's right' is confusing: a kid would not know what it means or when to tap it. 'Why do they get away with it?' is tempting for a bullied teen, and it seems to lead somewhere very different from 'Help.' That makes this question feel like a fork she can't see.
'A whole group of people' reads as a crowd or the public, not a clique at school. 'People with power over me' reads as a boss. None of the options says people my age, classmates or school.
Seven options, and several of them fit at once ('What they're saying about me', 'That it won't stop', 'That it keeps growing'). She has to pick one when two or three are true, which feels like a box.
'Something new just began' and 'Something hard just ended' sit next to scales of better and worse, so the list mixes two different kinds of answer.

results.overall: It was quick, and 'Help.' felt right to her. But most of the options were written for adults, so a bullied teenager kept tapping the nearest thing instead of the true thing. Adding 'Anxious', school and people her age would make it feel like it was about her.

verdict.why: Sofia feels anxious every morning on the bus and prays at night for it to stop, so "You're afraid, and you need something to hold on to" is plainly her and she would tap yes straight away. Psalm 118 suits her well. "What can man do to me?" speaks to a fear that other people cause, and the psalm goes on to describe being surrounded by those who push you to fall, which feels close to a group chat ganging up on her. "Whatever in you is afraid is strengthened by hope" is short and gentle enough for a 15-year-old to hold onto. Line 2, "help others take heart too", asks too much of her right now. Line 3 fits her night prayers, but it is weaker.
verdict.wouldHurt: There is a small risk. Read quickly, "What can man do to me?" could feel as if it waves away something that really is hurting her, because they are doing a lot to her. It helps that the psalm names people who attack as well as her fear. None of the three lines names what is actually happening to her, being mocked and humiliated by her peers, so she is seen as afraid rather than as mocked. If Athanasius's letter names a psalm for when people slander or mock you, offering it here would fit her better.
verdict.theirSituation: A 15-year-old being mocked in a group chat by girls at school, with screenshots passed around; she is hiding it from her parents and dreads going to school each morning.

results.desc: Luis, 41, Los Angeles, lapsed Catholic. Work is busy, the two kids have back-to-back activities, and the month has been fine, just full. He hasn't prayed properly in ages; God feels distant, but not in a painful way, more like an old friend he's lost touch with.

answers.wanted: Busy, but fine. Nothing's wrong, there's just a lot going on
Busy or stretched thin. "Worn out" sounds more drained than I am
Keeping up with work and the kids' schedules. It's everyday juggling, not worry about money or the future
Distant, like an old friend I've lost touch with. It's not painful, I just haven't made time
It's been a while. "I miss You" is a bit more emotional than I feel, but it's the nearest

friction.note: There's no 'busy' option. 'Pretty ordinary' undersells a packed month and 'Good' oversells it. Busy-but-fine is probably the most common state people are in, so it needs its own option.

The list leans toward strong emotions: afraid, heavy, angry, numb. It has nothing for mild everyday states like busy, distracted or fine. 'Worn out' was the only possible tap, and it pushes a normal busy person toward a tired or struggling reading.

Family life comes up only as 'Someone I care about', which sounds like worry about one person. Kids' activities and ordinary family logistics have nowhere to go. 'Work, money or what's next' packs three different things into one option.

'Far away' could mean painful abandonment or simple neglect, and the quiz can't tell which. It needs an option like 'I haven't really thought about Him lately' for the drifted-but-not-hurting person. 'Displeased with me' feels heavy and a bit preachy to a lapsed Catholic.

Almost every option is intense ('How long?', 'Help.', 'Why do they get away with it?', 'You decide who's right.'). The last two make no sense unless you're in a conflict, and they read as if the quiz expects a crisis. 'What do You want from me?' sounds accusatory. There's nothing for a casual reconnection like 'Hey, it's been a while' or 'I should talk to You more.' A lapsed person would feel all of these are a bit much.

The quiz feels built for people in strong spiritual or emotional situations: enemies, guilt, grief, praise. A fine-but-busy, drifted-away person has to round up to the nearest dramatic option on nearly every question, which could send him to a result about distress he doesn't feel.

results.overall: It was quick and easy to tap through, but as a busy guy whose life is fine and who has quietly drifted from God, I kept settling for the closest option rather than one that described me. The questions seem written for someone in trouble or on fire spiritually, not for an ordinary, full, distracted life.

verdict.why: Neither line is Luis. Line 1 says he longs for God's house, but he doesn't: he has drifted from God without feeling any ache about it. Tapping yes would claim a hunger he doesn't have. Line 2 says life has left him poor, empty and listless. His month has been fine, just full. Busy is not worn down, and calling it affliction misreads him. Both lines assume strong feeling, either longing or exhaustion. Nothing covers the plain case of being "fine, busy, and out of touch with God." The fallback page is worse. "What you're going through" and all three routes (grinding me down, weighing on me, making me afraid) assume something is wrong. Nothing is wrong for Luis. He would feel boxed into a negative answer, which is the same funnelling the owner complained about in Question 1. Psalm 42 ("Where is your God?") could honestly speak to drifting from God. But it is offered as "it's weighing on me, and it won't lift," which Luis would not pick. The quiz needs a neutral path for people whose life is simply full and whose faith has gone quiet. It should also give a positive answer as much weight as a negative one.
verdict.theirSituation: His life is busy and fine, and he has drifted from God the way you lose touch with an old friend: it is distant but doesn't hurt, and nothing is wrong enough to call suffering or longing.

results.desc: Hannah, 33, Leeds, UK, Baptist. Her first baby is six weeks old, and she is exhausted and very happy in about equal measure. She can't concentrate long enough to pray and feels a bit guilty that she hasn't been to church since the birth.

answers.wanted: Exhausting but happy. It's not up and down, it's both at once, all day
Tired but happy. I had to pick between Worn out and Glad, and both are equally true
My baby / my new family. 'Someone I care about' sounds like I'm worried about someone, and 'Someone in my life' could also have been it
I honestly haven't had the headspace to notice. Not far, just crowded out
Thank You, and sorry I've been so absent. Thanks is true, but a bit of guilt goes with it
For them to be healthy and grow up well / to be kept safe. All three options assume the person is suffering, and my baby is fine
A new baby. 'A new home' and 'Someone coming to faith' are there but a new baby or a new relationship isn't, so I tapped 'Everything, really'

friction.note: There's no answer for a good time that is also draining. 'Up and down' suggests mood swings, but new parents, carers and people starting new jobs feel both things at once. Something like 'Tiring, but good' would catch a lot of people.

Only one word allowed. The list has six negative words (Afraid, Heavy, Worn out, Angry, Numb, Restless) and three positive ones, so a happy but tired person gets pushed toward the negative side. Letting people pick two, or adding 'Tired but happy', would fix that.
'Someone in my life' and 'Someone I care about' are too close to tell apart. I couldn't work out which one covers my baby. Both read like there's a problem with that person.

Every option (Comfort, A way out or healing, Someone to help them) assumes the loved one is in trouble. If they're a newborn, a new partner or a child doing well, nothing fits. 'For them to be safe and well' or 'That they grow up well' would cover the happy cases.

There's no option for 'I haven't had room to think about it.' 'Far away' and 'Silent' put the distance on God. 'Near, but quiet' is the kindest choice but claims more than I feel. A lot of busy people will be in this spot.

'Why do they get away with it?' and 'You decide who's right.' feel oddly specific next to the others, like they're steering toward particular psalms. I also couldn't say two things at once (Thank You plus I'm sorry).

'A new home' and 'Someone coming to faith' are very specific life events, but more common ones are missing: a new baby, a new marriage, a new job, recovering from illness. Having 'A new home' there makes the missing baby stand out. 'I'm growing' is vague.

This question never came up for me, but I feel mild guilt about not praying or going to church. Nothing in the quiz lets me say that gently. The only route is 'I'm sorry' or 'Displeased with me', and both feel too heavy for 'I've been busy with a newborn.'

results.overall: It was quick and mostly friendly, but I kept having to choose between the tired half and the happy half of my life when both are true. The follow-ups assumed the person I love is in trouble, so it felt built for people who are struggling rather than for a happy but exhausted new mum.

verdict.why: Line 1 half-fits, because I am worn down, but "poor, empty and listless" isn't me. I'm exhausted, not empty, and I'm happier than I've ever been, so I'd say "Not quite". Line 2 is about someone else being in trouble, and nobody is. Line 3 is the one I'd tap "Yes" on. The baby is the biggest thing I've ever had to thank God for, and "in and through everything" covers the 3am feeds too. Psalm 103 would really land for me: "as a father has compassion on his children", and "He knows our frame; He remembers that we are dust" (103:13-14) would ease my guilt about not managing to pray or get to church. The line itself says nothing about that guilt or the tiredness, though, so it fits me well enough without quite seeing me.
verdict.wouldHurt: Nothing in Psalm 103 would hurt. Two smaller problems: being shown "poor, empty and listless" first, as my best match, feels like the quiz read my happy exhaustion as depression, and that is a mild misread. And the line and Athanasius's words present thanks as something I "ought" to give, which could add to my guilt instead of easing it unless the page points to the compassion verses (103:13-14).
verdict.theirSituation: A new mother who is joyful and exhausted in equal measure, grateful for her baby but guilty that she can't concentrate to pray or get to church.

results.desc: Chidi, 27, Lagos, Nigeria, Anglican. He just accepted a job in Abuja and is moving next month, leaving friends and his church behind. He is excited and nervous and already feels a bit lonely thinking about starting over.

answers.wanted: Exciting but scary, big change coming
Something new is about to begin (the move is next month, it hasn't started yet)
Excited and nervous at the same time; a bit lonely already
Good to me, but I'm about to leave them behind
Go with me / Don't let me be alone there
A fresh start, a new job in a new city

friction.note: No option for a big change that is exciting and scary at once. 'Up and down' suggests a rough patch that swings, not anticipation. I switched between 'Good' and 'Up and down'.

'Just began' is the only option for change, but the move hasn't happened yet. Nothing covers something about to start. Putting 'Something hard just ended' in the same list as 'Getting worse or better' mixes two different kinds of answer.

Choosing a single word leaves out mixed feelings. 'Excited' and 'Nervous' (or 'Hopeful') are missing, and those are the two most common feelings before a move. Seven of the nine words are heavy or negative, so a positive-but-anxious person has little to pick from.
There's nothing for 'good people I'm about to leave'. 'Far away, or gone' sounds like death or estrangement, not a friendly goodbye.

'Why do they get away with it?' and 'You decide who's right' seem out of the blue for most people. 'How great You are' reads as churchy. The list lacks a plain request for God's company, like 'Be with me' or 'Go before me', which is the one thing someone starting over would say.

'A new home' and 'Someone coming to faith' are very specific and feel like slots made for particular psalms. 'A new home' almost fit, but I was really thinking of a new job and a fresh start. 'How good and well-made everything is' is odd wording.

results.overall: The quiz was quick and mostly easy on a phone. But it seems built for people either suffering or content, and it has no room for someone who is excited, nervous and a little lonely before a move. I got through it by picking the nearest options instead of ones that described me.

verdict.why: As Chidi, I'd say yes to line 1, but only half-heartedly. I really am thankful for the job, and "thank God in everything" is how a Lagos Anglican would talk about a new post. So it isn't wrong, but it only sees the excited half of me. It doesn't touch leaving my friends and church, the nerves, or the loneliness I can already feel coming. Line 3 is actually closer to my real situation: a new home and giving myself to God in a new place. But "you've just moved" is simply false, because I move next month. It reads as oddly specific, like a box I almost fit, so I'd tap "Not quite" on it out of honesty. Line 2 is too heavy. I'm not downcast, I'm unsettled. Psalm 103 ("do not forget all His kind deeds") would bless me and wouldn't hurt, but it would feel generic, like a psalm for any good week. What's missing is an option about a threshold: grateful to be going, sad about what I'm leaving, nervous about starting over. The quiz saw my gratitude but not my transition. The fix is either to word line 3 more loosely ("You're starting over somewhere new, and you want to give it to God") or to add a leaving/new-start option, which Athanasius's letter may support.
verdict.theirSituation: He's about to move to a new city for a job he's grateful for, but he's nervous and already grieving the friends and church he's leaving. That's a threshold moment, and no line names it: "thankful" catches half of it, and "just moved into a new home" is wrong on timing and too narrow.

results.desc: Margaret, 68, Des Moines, Iowa, Lutheran. She retired from teaching in June after thirty-eight years, and the days feel shapeless. She is grateful and rested, but she keeps wondering what she's actually for now.

answers.wanted: Good, but unsettled. Restful and nice, just without much shape to it.
A big change: I retired. Something ended (my career) and something new began at the same time, and I'm not sure 'new began' is right when nothing has started yet.
Grateful but a bit lost. I'm both grateful and restless and could only pick one; 'Unsettled' or 'Adrift' would fit best.
What would You have me do now? / Show me what's next. 'What do You want from me?' sounds exasperated, and I'm not frustrated with Him, just asking.

More time and rest, a new chapter. Also, I'm not sure what 'it' means here. My season is good because I've retired and I'm rested, and none of the options (being led, a new home, someone coming to faith) fit that. 'I can see Him leading me' would be the opposite of how I feel.

friction.note: Five of the six options are simple ratings, but real life is often 'good but aimless'. Nothing describes a calm, pleasant season that lacks direction.

'Something hard just ended' and 'Something new just began' sit awkwardly beside 'worse / same / better'. They answer a different question, and a retirement is both an ending and a beginning, but not a hard one.

Only one word can be picked, and people often feel two things at once. Several of the nine words are heavy (Afraid, Heavy, Angry, Numb), so the list tilts toward distress. There is no word for 'unsettled', 'adrift' or 'curious'.

'Work, money or what's next' groups three different worries together. For me only 'what's next' fits, and money doesn't come into it. 'Someone in my life' and 'Someone I care about' are hard to tell apart.
'Talking behind my back' is oddly specific next to the others.

The options mix gentle ones with sharp or accusing ones ('Why do they get away with it?', 'You decide who's right.'). 'What do You want from me?' reads as angry even when you mean it as a sincere question. The list could use a calm, open request such as 'Show me the way' or 'What now?'.

'What's behind it?' doesn't say what 'it' is. I got here because of 'Something new just began', but the options assume the new thing is a spiritual blessing. 'A new home' and 'Someone coming to faith' are hyper-specific and feel like boxes. There is nothing for a life change like retirement, a new job or an empty nest, or for 'more time and rest'.

results.overall: The core questions were quick, and most of them landed near enough. But as someone who is content yet directionless, I kept being made to choose between hard and good, and the one follow-up I got felt built for someone else. By the end I suspected the quiz would read my retirement as a blessing story or a trouble story, not as a question about what I'm for now.

verdict.why: As Margaret: line 1 misses. It asks whether I'm becoming the right kind of person, and I'm not worried about that; I'm wondering what I'm for now that the work is over. Line 2 is wrong because nothing is weighing on me: I'm rested and grateful, and the days are just shapeless. Line 3 is the first one I'd say yes to, because I really am thankful for thirty-eight years and a good retirement. Psalm 103 would speak to me more than the line suggests. "Forget not all His benefits" fits a woman looking back on a career. "Renews your youth like the eagle's" and "as for man, his days are like grass" touch the season I'm in. But I'd be saying yes to the grateful half of me, not to the question that brought me to the quiz. No line names a purpose question like "wondering what you're for now", and that is the real gap. If I said "Not quite" to all three, the fallback would miss me completely. All three routes are about distress ("grinding me down", "afraid"), and I'm not suffering. I'm unmoored. I'd feel I had been sorted into a crisis I don't have.
verdict.wouldHurt: Nothing in Psalm 103 would wound her. The risk is that it only affirms her gratitude and leaves out the real question of what she's for now, so it feels pleasant but beside the point. The fallback is a different matter: if she had turned down all three, each route assumes trouble (grinding, afraid, won't lift). That would misread a content, grateful retiree as someone in distress.
verdict.theirSituation: A grateful, rested retiree who is not in trouble but has lost her sense of purpose and is asking what God wants her for in this new, unstructured season.

results.desc: Nikos, 45, Athens, Greece, nominal Orthodox. He goes to church at Easter and for weddings and funerals, and lately he's been reading about science and wondering whether any of it holds up. He isn't upset, just unsure, and quietly curious whether God is there at all.

answers.wanted: Curious, or Unsure. He isn't restless in a troubled way, just quietly thinking things over. A plain "Fine" or "Thoughtful" would also have worked.
Whether God is there at all, or "Big questions: what's true". He isn't asking where he stands with Him. He's asking whether there's a Him to stand with.
I'm not sure He's there, or I don't really know
Are You there?, or Show me You're real. Otherwise a way to pass, like "Nothing, really" or "I'm not sure what I'd say".

friction.note: "And God, right now, feels…" takes it as given that God is there and can be felt. For someone who doubts, every option pushes him to act as if he believes. There is no neutral choice like "I'm not sure He's there" or "I don't really think about it".

The question asks him to speak to God directly, and every answer is a believer's prayer: lament, sorrow, thanks or praise. A curious sceptic has nothing to pick. It feels like a box, and a little preachy. "What do You want from me?" sounds pleading or angry, which is not his mood at all. It needs a doubting option ("Are You there?") or an honest opt-out.

"God, and where I stand with Him" is about a relationship with God, not about whether God exists. It is close, but it frames his question as a personal standing issue. Something like "Big questions about God and faith" would catch far more people.

The list moves from negatives (afraid, heavy, worn out, angry, numb, restless) straight to calm, grateful and glad. There is nothing for the plain middle, like "Okay", "Thoughtful", "Curious" or "Unsure". Six of the nine words are negative, so a neutral person gets nudged toward a darker word like Restless.

"Something hard just ended" and "Something new just began" sit next to a worse / same / better scale. They are a different kind of answer, so the list reads as mixed and uneven, though it didn't stop him.
"Displeased with me" and "Clearly at work" are church-insider phrases. A nominal Orthodox man would find them odd, as if they were written for someone more devout than him.

results.overall: The first half felt easy and neutral. From the God questions on, it assumed a believer praying, and he had no honest option for "I'm not sure He's there". He finished it, but his last answer was forced, and he wouldn't trust that the result was about him.

verdict.why: None of the three lines fits a calm, curious doubter. Line 1 assumes I long for God's house. I go at Easter, and I'm not longing for anything. Line 2 is about whether I'm becoming the right kind of person, but my question comes before that: is God there at all? Line 3 says something is weighing on my soul, and I already said I'm not upset. The fallback is worse. It opens with "what you're going through" and only offers ways it is hurting me (grinding me down, weighing on me, making me afraid). None of those is true, so I'd leave feeling my question was treated as a crisis to manage. That boxes me in: every exit is either longing or pain, with no neutral road for "I'm just wondering". This matches the owner's complaint that the answers funnel you toward the negative. The quiz needs a neutral path for questioning and wondering, and it should not end on psalms that call the doubter a fool.
verdict.wouldHurt: Not much in the three lines. The fallback assumes I'm suffering ("what it's doing to you", three kinds of pain). That misreads calm curiosity as distress, and if the crisis line (988) shows up on that path, it would feel patronising.
verdict.theirSituation: He is calm and curious, reading about science and quietly wondering whether God is real. He isn't grieving, longing or struggling, so he needs a neutral route for honest questions rather than one for pain or devotion.

results.desc: Ana, 36, Manila, Philippines, Catholic. Life is steady: work, family, the usual. She still says the rosary most nights out of habit but has felt nothing for months, and she wonders whether that's normal or whether something is wrong with her.

answers.wanted: Something like 'Flat' or 'Going through the motions'. My life is fine; it's only my prayer that feels numb, and 'Numb' on its own sounds like I'm depressed.
'Are You still there?' or 'Is this normal?' I don't miss Him like after a loss. I just feel nothing and wonder if something is wrong with me.

friction.note: The list mixes moods about life (afraid, angry, glad) with how prayer feels. When life is steady but faith feels dry, no word fits both. 'Numb' reads as a clinical or depressive word.

There is no quiet or uncertain option, like 'I don't know what to say' or 'Are You there?'. 'Why do they get away with it?' and 'You decide who's right.' are very specific to a conflict and feel like they come from a different quiz. Most options are strong emotional outbursts, and someone whose prayer has gone flat does not feel any of them.
'Displeased with me' may push a worried Catholic toward guilt. There is no option like 'I can't tell' for someone who honestly doesn't know.

None of the follow-ups triggered for her, so the quiz never asks about the actual situation: praying out of habit and feeling nothing. It seems to have no way to tell spiritual dryness apart from grief or conflict.
'Against me' and 'Talking behind my back' are strong options. For an ordinary person they stand out as oddly specific, while the neutral choices are thin.

results.overall: The quiz was quick, and the first few questions and the focus question fit her well. By the last question she felt the options were written for people in crisis or conflict, with nowhere to say that her prayer has gone flat and she wonders whether that's normal. She had to settle for 'I miss You', which doesn't quite fit.

verdict.why: As Ana, I would say "Not quite" to both lines. Line 1 describes longing for God's house, but my problem is that I feel no longing at all. I would read it and think "I wish," not "that's me." Line 2 gets the emptiness and listlessness right, but it starts with "Life has worn you down," and my life isn't wearing me down. Work and family are steady. What's wrong is my prayer: I say the rosary and feel nothing. Line 2 describes someone crushed by life, and that isn't me. The fallback would half-work. "It's weighing on me, and it won't lift" (Psalm 42) sounds too heavy, because I'm not in distress, just puzzled and a little worried. Still, once opened, Psalm 42 is the right psalm: "As the deer pants for the water brooks... Why are you downcast, O my soul?" It is the classic psalm for spiritual dryness, and it would quietly answer my question of whether this is normal. The problem is that the quiz sends me there through a label that overstates my situation. The fallback's opening, "Athanasius's letter doesn't name what you're going through," also feels off. Feeling far from God while still praying is one of the most ordinary Christian experiences. If I recall Athanasius's letter correctly (worth checking), he pairs longing or thirsting for God with Psalms 42 and 63, so a line like "You keep praying, but God feels far off and you feel nothing" could lead there directly. This fits the owner's note: none of the question paths or results give the plain middle case, a steady life with a dry prayer life.
verdict.wouldHurt: Psalm 102's "poor, empty, worn down to listlessness" and "afflicted, withered like grass" make my situation sound like suffering. Coming just after I told the quiz I wonder whether something is wrong with me, that could confirm the fear instead of easing it. The fallback's "doesn't name what you're going through" also tells me my experience is unusual when it is common. That is the opposite of the reassurance I came for.
verdict.theirSituation: Her life is steady and she keeps up her prayer out of habit, but for months she has felt nothing, and she wants to know whether that dryness is normal. She is not grieving, afraid or worn down by her circumstances.

results.desc: Ben, 22, Minneapolis, Minnesota, became a Christian six months ago through a campus group. The early excitement has worn off and he's not sure he is doing it right; reading the Bible is harder than he expected. He believes, but God feels quieter than at the start.

answers.wanted: Kind of flat, honestly. Not bad, just not like it was.
It's cooled off since the start
Unsure, or flat
Quieter than He used to be
Am I doing this right?

friction.note: Nothing fits a slow fade. 'Getting worse' is too dramatic and 'About the same' isn't true. A 'Cooled off' or 'Less than it was' option would catch a lot of people like me.
The options jump between big emotions (afraid, angry, numb). There's nothing for mild, low-key states like unsure, flat, bored or distracted, and I bet most people are in one of those.
'Displeased with me' reads as heavy church talk. There's no 'I'm not sure' or 'Quieter than before' option, which is exactly how God feels to a new believer when the first excitement wears off.

Most options assume a crisis or enemies. 'Why do they get away with it?' and 'You decide who's right' made no sense for my life, and 'How long?' sounds like someone suffering. There's no plain questioning option like 'Am I doing this right?' or 'Show me what's next.' 'What do You want from me?' sounds angry, not curious.
The scale is fine, but 'Up and down' and 'Pretty ordinary' both half-fit. A calm, slightly flat season falls between them.
'God, and where I stand with Him' fit, but it's the only option that points at faith, so it feels a bit on the nose.

results.overall: It was quick and mostly easy to tap through, but as a new believer in a quiet, cooling-off stretch I kept settling for the nearest option. The answer sets lean toward crisis, enemies or big feelings and leave little room for 'things are fine but flat and I'm unsure'. None of the follow-ups triggered, so the result probably rests on thin signal.

verdict.why: As Ben I would tap "Not quite" on line 1. Longing for God's house and a home that lasts forever sounds like heaven or church buildings. What I actually miss is how close God felt six months ago. Line 2 is too heavy for me. I'm not downcast, and nothing is "weighing on my soul" like grief. I'm just flat and unsure I'm doing it right. Still, it's the closer of the two, and the fallback's three choices all assume some trouble is happening to me, so I'd accept line 2 without much conviction. The psalm itself fits me better than the line that led to it. "As the deer pants," thirst for God, "these things I remember... how I used to go with the throng" and "Why are you downcast... put your hope in God" describe my faded early excitement and quieter God almost exactly. The quiz needs a line in my own words, something like "God feels further away than He used to, and you miss how it was at the start." That would point to Psalm 42 without making me sound depressed.
verdict.wouldHurt: "Won't lift" makes an ordinary dry spell sound like depression or heavy grief. A new believer might read it as a sign that something is wrong with his faith. If this path also shows the 988 crisis line, that would feel badly out of proportion for Ben.
verdict.theirSituation: A new believer whose first excitement has faded. He isn't in trouble. God just feels quieter, the Bible is harder than he expected, and he misses how close God felt at the start.

results.desc: Ruth, 50, Bristol, UK, Methodist. Her fourteen-year-old dog has kidney failure and the vet says it's probably a matter of weeks. Otherwise life is fine, but she feels silly for how much it's weighing on her and hasn't mentioned it to anyone but her sister.

answers.wanted: Mostly fine, apart from one sad thing
Had some bad news recently
Someone I'm about to lose (my dog)
Near, but I haven't really talked to Him about it
Please help me through this / give me strength to let go

friction.note: No option for 'life is fine except for one thing'. 'Up and down' and 'Hard, but I'm getting by' both overstate it, and she already feels silly for how much it weighs on her.
'Getting worse' sounds like her whole life is getting worse. The real change is one piece of bad news, and there is no option like 'Something hard is coming'.

There is nothing for a loss that is coming but hasn't happened, and nothing for a pet. 'Someone or something I've lost' is too early, and 'Someone I care about' makes her wonder whether a dog counts. Anticipatory grief is common, so it deserves its own option.
'Against me' and 'Talking behind my back' feel dramatic and oddly specific at the top of the list. Most people would skim straight past them.

'Why do they get away with it?' and 'You decide who's right.' feel like they come from a very particular situation, and reading them makes the quiz feel like it is fishing for enemies. There is nothing gentle like 'Give me strength' or 'Please be with me'.
'Someone to help them' is odd for a pet or for someone past help. The follow-up only half fits here: what she wants is for the dog not to suffer and for herself to cope.

results.overall: Quick and mostly gentle, but Ruth kept settling for near-misses. The quiz seems built for enemies, sin or big crises, and it has no plain place for a small, private sadness like a dying pet. That made her feel a bit silly again, as though her grief didn't quite count.

verdict.why: As Ruth, the first line doesn't fit. I'm not pleading with God. I've accepted what the vet said and I'm not asking for a miracle for a fourteen-year-old dog, so it's "Not quite". The second line is the one: something is weighing on me, it won't lift, and it's weighing more than I think it should. I'd tap "Yes, that's it". I wouldn't reach the third line. It's close, since someone I love is in trouble, but a dog isn't someone I'd pray over with Psalm 20, and it would feel odd. Psalm 42 suits the mood. It speaks to my own soul ("Why are you downcast?"), and "my tears have been my food" is there without anyone telling me I'm being silly. Because it doesn't name the dog or loss, it doesn't box me in. It's generic enough to fit, and it gently treats the heaviness as worth bringing to God. The only gap is that this is grief before a loss, and the psalm is about longing for God, not losing a companion. So it speaks to me, but sideways.
verdict.theirSituation: She is quietly grieving ahead of time for a dying old dog and feels embarrassed by how much it hurts. She isn't pleading for an outcome; she's carrying a sadness she thinks she shouldn't feel this much.

results.desc: Mina, 31, Cairo, Egypt, Coptic Orthodox. It has been an ordinary, slightly boring week: work, the gym, dinner with his parents on Friday. Nothing is wrong, but everything feels like routine, and he wonders if there's meant to be more to faith than turning up.

answers.wanted: Bored, or Flat. It's a low-key 'meh', not restless energy
Whether there's more to all this / feeling stuck in a routine. 'Where I stand with Him' sounds like guilt, and that isn't what I mean
Same as always, like a habit. Not far, not close, just part of the routine
Is there more than this? / Show me more. 'What do You want from me?' sounds exasperated or frustrated, and I'm not

friction.note: Every word except Calm is strong: Afraid, Heavy, Angry, Numb. There's no mild 'Bored' or 'Flat' for an ordinary week, so the list pushes a normal person toward drama or toward Calm.

'God, and where I stand with Him' sounds like being on trial. Someone who is just wondering if faith should feel like more has nothing that fits. 'Work, money or what's next' is close but misses the faith part.

Three of the seven options are about hostility ('Against me', 'Talking behind my back', 'Hard to be around'). That's a lot for a question most people will answer 'Fine' to. It shows the quiz is looking for enemies.
Nothing for 'the same as usual / routine'. 'Silent' and 'Far away' are too negative. 'Near, but quiet' is too warm for someone just going through the motions.

This is the most box-like question. Almost every line is a crisis or a specific drama ('Why do they get away with it?', 'You decide who's right.', 'How long?'). An ordinary person gets only 'Thank You', 'How great You are', or the testy 'What do You want from me?'. It needs something like 'Show me more' or 'Is this all there is?'.
'Why do they get away with it?' and 'You decide who's right.' assume a 'they' that most people taking this won't have. They read as oddly specific.

results.overall: The first two questions were easy and felt fair for an ordinary week. After that it felt like the quiz expected me to be in trouble: most of the options were about enemies, guilt or crisis. I kept picking the nearest mild option rather than the true one, so I doubt the psalm I'd get would really be about my situation, which is feeling a bit stuck in a routine faith.

verdict.why: As Mina, line 1 is the only one near me. "Whether you are becoming one" catches my quiet question: is showing up enough, or should I be growing into something? I would tap "Yes, that's it", though a little hesitantly. The line is framed around belonging and worthiness, and I am not anxious about whether I belong. I'm restless, going through the motions, wanting more depth. Psalm 15 answers "more than turning up" with a list of how to live: speak truth, keep your word, don't slander. That is a fair and useful answer, and nothing in it hurts. It points me outward from routine into how I treat people, which is real. But it doesn't name what I feel, which is the flatness of an ordinary week and a faith that has become habit. Line 2 would misread me, because nothing is weighing on my soul. The fallback would be worse. All three options (grinding, weighing, afraid) assume something is wrong, and there is no honest option for "nothing is wrong, it's just routine." That is the same negative funnel the owner described in Question 1.
verdict.wouldHurt: Nothing wounds, but the worthiness framing ("belongs with God") could read as a check on whether I am good enough, when my actual state is restlessness and dryness, not guilt.
verdict.theirSituation: Mina is fine, just in a routine week where faith feels like habit, and he wonders whether there is meant to be more to it than showing up.

results.desc: Carmen, 63, Lima, Peru, Catholic. Her daughter started speaking to her again after six years apart, and they had lunch last week. She is happy and thankful, but the conversation was awkward and some of the old hurt is still there on both sides.

answers.wanted: Good, better than in years, but still tender
Someone came back into my life (it is both something hard ending and something new beginning, and I could only pick one)
My daughter and me, the two of us. I nearly tapped "Someone in my life" and could not tell how it differs from "Someone I care about"
Closer than before, but it's still awkward
For the old hurt between us to heal (I only tapped this because of the word "healing"; "a way out" sounds like she is in danger)
Years apart from someone I love. Every option is about enemies, trouble, God or my own sin, and a daughter who stopped speaking to me is none of those

friction.note: "Something hard just ended" and "Something new just began" are both true for a reconciliation, and you can pick only one. Real turning points are often both.
"Someone in my life" and "Someone I care about" read the same. A mother does not know whether her daughter is "in my life" or "someone I care about", so the pair feels like a trick.

It asks about "the people around you" as one group, but for her one relationship matters and it is mixed. The list jumps from "Hard to be around" straight to "Fine" and "Kind", with nothing for "better, but still awkward".

Four of the five options are dark and specific (people against me, God against me, something I'd done), which feels like being pushed into an enemies or guilt story. There is nothing for an ordinary life event such as an estrangement, a separation or a long wait.
"A way out, or healing" puts escape and healing together. "Someone to help them" suggests the loved one is helpless. Nothing fits wanting a relationship to heal.
Nothing fits good but mixed, happy and hurting at once. "Up and down" sounds more unstable than she feels.
Hardly any answer lets her say that joy and old hurt are both there. The quiz assumes one mood, while her real situation is gratitude with a bruise.

results.overall: Carmen found it gentle and quick, and the questions on God and on what she would say to Him fit her exactly. But she had to squeeze a happy reconciliation that still hurts into single-mood answers. The "What was it?" follow-up only offered enemies, trouble or guilt, and that felt like being pushed into a box that is not her life.

verdict.why: Thankfulness is what Carmen feels most about her daughter coming back after six years, so line 1 is the first one she would say yes to. "In and through everything" even leaves room for the awkward lunch and the hurt that is still there. Psalm 103 speaks to her more than its opening line shows: it talks about God not keeping His anger forever, removing sins as far as the east is from the west, and having compassion like a father on his children. Those verses are about reconciliation and fit a mother and daughter who are finding their way back. Line 2 does not fit because she is not pleading. Line 3 would misread her because she does not see the six years as God testing her, and the hurt is not over. The one gap is that line 1 does not name the mixed feeling, being thankful while it is still tender. She would still feel mostly seen, not boxed in.
verdict.theirSituation: She is thankful that her daughter is speaking to her again after six years, but it is still fragile, awkward and sore on both sides.

results.desc: Samuel, 38, Chennai, India, Church of South India. He has a job offer in Dubai with much better pay, but it means leaving his aging parents and his wife's family. He has been praying about it for weeks and feels no clear answer either way.

answers.wanted: At a crossroads / facing a big decision. My life isn't up and down, it's stuck on one choice.
Something big has come up that I have to decide. Nothing has begun yet; it's an offer I haven't taken.
Torn, or unsure
Show me which way to go. / Which way should I go? Guidance, not frustration.
A job offer, a big choice. The question assumes something good is behind my situation, and nothing is. I'm undecided.

friction.note: The options only measure how good or bad life feels. There's nothing for someone who isn't suffering or thriving, just standing at a fork. Big decisions like a move, a job or a marriage are common, and none of the six options covers them.
'Something new just began' is the nearest option for a decision that's still pending, but it isn't accurate. There's no 'Something big has come up' or 'I'm waiting on something.'

Tapping 'Something new just began' sends me to 'What's behind it?', which assumes the new thing is a blessing. Every option is positive and specific ('A new home', 'Someone coming to faith'). Coming right after I said God feels silent, 'I can see Him leading me' reads like it's pushing me toward a cheerful answer.

'What do You want from me?' sounds exasperated or accusatory. A sincere person asking for direction would want a gentle version like 'Show me the way' or 'What should I do?' The list has lament, guilt, justice and praise, but nothing that simply asks for guidance.
My worry is split between work and leaving my aging parents ('Someone I care about'). I can only pick one, so half of what's really on my mind gets lost.
Only 3 of the 9 words are neutral or positive, and nothing covers being torn, unsure or uncertain. 'Restless' suggests agitation more than indecision.
There's no option for people who are kind but pulling in different directions (family who'd be hurt if I leave). 'Kind to me' is true but misses the tension.

results.overall: The quiz was quick and mostly easy to answer, but it seemed built for people who are clearly suffering or clearly blessed. As a man stuck on a decision and waiting on God, I had to settle for near-enough options on almost every question, and the follow-up forced me to pick a happy reason for something that isn't settled yet.

verdict.why: Line 1 misses: I am not asking whether I am becoming a godly person. I am asking which way God wants me to go. Line 3 is plainly wrong. I have not moved house. I am only thinking about a move, so it reads as if the quiz took "moving" from my answers and jumped ahead. Line 2 is the closest. The decision has weighed on me for weeks, and Psalm 42 has "Why the unease within me?" and "Put your hope in God". Its cry of "where is your God?" also fits praying and hearing nothing back. I would tap yes to it, a little reluctantly. What I am really living is not being able to discern God's will: torn between better pay and duty to my aging parents, and waiting on God. None of the lines names that. A line like "You're facing a choice and asking God to show you the way, and He hasn't answered yet" would have been exactly me.
verdict.wouldHurt: It won't wound me, but it misreads me a little. "Weighing on your soul, and it won't lift" and "downcast" sound like sorrow or depression. I am not depressed. I am torn and waiting. The new-home line feels slightly careless, like the quiz heard "move" and assumed it had already happened.
verdict.theirSituation: He is torn over a big decision: a better-paid job abroad or staying near his aging parents. He has prayed for weeks without a clear answer, so what he needs is guidance and patience while he waits on God, not comfort for sorrow.

results.desc: Kayla, 17, Savannah, Georgia, grew up going to a Methodist church. She is stressed about college applications and her SAT scores, but otherwise things are fine with friends and family. She believes in God, though right now it's more background than anything she thinks about.

answers.wanted: Stressful. Busy and stressed, but nothing's actually wrong
More stressful, with deadlines coming up, but nothing bad happened. 'Getting worse' sounds like my life is falling apart, and it isn't
Stressed, or anxious. 'Afraid' is too strong and 'Restless' isn't quite it either
Honestly, I haven't really thought about it. He's just kind of there in the background
Please let this work out, or help me get into a good school. 'Help.' works, but it sounds more desperate than I feel

friction.note: Nothing fits normal, everyday stress. 'Hard, but I'm getting by' sounds too serious and 'Up and down' isn't really it. A word like 'Busy' or 'Stressful' is missing, and that's where lots of students and working adults would land.

'Something hard just ended' and 'Something new just began' feel oddly specific next to the others. Senior year starting could count as 'new', which is confusing. Nothing covers 'the pressure is building'.

The list jumps from strong negative words (Afraid, Angry, Numb) to calm and positive ones, and the everyday middle is missing: stressed, anxious, busy, distracted. For a teenager, 'Stressed' is the obvious word to look for.

'Work, money or what's next' fits, but only because of 'what's next'. A teenager doesn't think about work or money, so the option feels written for adults. 'School, work or my future' would read better.

It assumes you feel God one way or another right now. Everything from 'Displeased with me' to 'Clearly at work' supposes you've been paying attention. There's no neutral 'I haven't thought about it much', so a background believer has to pick a feeling she doesn't have.

Most of the options are dramatic lines from the Psalms ('Why do they get away with it?', 'You decide who's right.', 'How long?'). They feel like they belong to a particular kind of person, and a normal teen would read past them. The list goes from crisis to praise with little in between, like 'Please let this go well' or 'Give me peace'. 'You decide who's right' makes no sense unless you're in a fight with someone.
Mostly fine. 'Talking behind my back' next to 'Against me' feels a bit specific, but those are easy to skip.

results.overall: It's quick and easy on a phone. But as a stressed senior with a pretty normal life, I kept looking for words like 'stressed' or 'busy' and settling for the nearest option instead. The questions about God and what I'd say to Him seem written for someone in a crisis or someone very devout, not someone for whom God is in the background.

verdict.why: As Kayla, I wouldn't say yes to either line. Line 1 describes someone who is "poor, empty and listless" and forgets to eat, and that's far heavier than where I am. I'm stressed about the SAT and applications, but I have energy, my friends and family are fine, and I'm not empty. Saying yes would mean pretending to a despair I don't feel. Line 2 assumes I want to plead with God and I'm looking for words to pray. Right now God is in the background for me, so that line describes someone more devout, or more desperate, than I am. The fallback is closer. "It's making me afraid" (the fear of rejection and of not getting in) or "It's weighing on me" is something I'd tap. Psalm 118 ("The LORD is with me; I will not be afraid") could actually land for a stressed senior. But being told "Athanasius's letter doesn't name what you're going through" feels odd for something as ordinary as exam stress. It makes my normal worry sound like an unusual crisis. The larger problem is that the quiz seems to have steered me toward affliction and pleading, with no line for everyday pressure about the future. That fits the owner's complaint that answers funnel toward the negative with no neutral middle.
verdict.theirSituation: A 17-year-old whose life is basically fine but who is anxious about SAT scores and college applications, and whose faith is quietly in the background rather than something she's actively praying through.

results.desc: Paul, 60, Birmingham, Alabama, Episcopalian. He picked up his five-year sobriety chip last week, and his grown son came to watch. He feels grateful in a way that still surprises him and wants to keep saying thank you to God.

answers.wanted: Something I've been working at for years just hit a milestone. Things are steady-good, not newly better, and the hard part didn't 'just end'.
How far I've come / what God has done for me. 'Where I stand with Him' sounds like I'm worried about it, and I'm not.
He pulled me out of something and has kept me out of it. It's rescue from a long time ago, and staying rescued, not general kindness or 'I'm growing'.

friction.note: No option for a milestone or anniversary. 'Something hard just ended' doesn't fit a recovery that ended five years ago and is still going on. The rescue-and-deliverance route (the 'how did it end' follow-ups) only opens if the hard thing is recent, so long-term gratitude for being delivered has no way in.
'Someone in my life' and 'Someone I care about' read as the same thing. My son is both. It's not clear which one to tap.

'God, and where I stand with Him' leans anxious, like I'm being checked up on. A grateful person has no plain positive option here. The list is mostly problems (health, money, loss, the world), so a good season gets pushed to 'Nothing in particular' or a worried-sounding choice.
Seven of the nine options are complaints or pleas and only two are positive, so it's lopsided. 'You decide who's right' is an odd thing to say to God and would confuse most people.

The options are a mix of very specific items ('A new home', 'Someone coming to faith') and very vague ones ('Everything, really'). Nothing covers being set free from something or given a second chance, which is the most common reason people feel this grateful. 'How good and well-made everything is' sounds like a nature walk, not a life.
The scale jumps from 'Fine' to 'Kind to me' to 'A real gift'. That works, but the negative side has four shades and the positive side has two, which matches the imbalance the owner described.

results.overall: It was quick and mostly easy for Paul, and 'Thank You' and 'Clearly at work' felt right. But nearly every question is built around trouble, so a steadily grateful man in recovery had to pick near-misses: no milestone option, a focus that sounds worried, and nothing for 'He set me free and kept me free' in the follow-up.

verdict.why: Paul's whole state right now is gratitude that keeps surprising him, and he wants to keep thanking God. "You want to thank God, in and through everything" says that plainly, in words he would use himself, so he would tap yes on the first line. "In and through everything" also fits a man in recovery: he is grateful for the hard years too, because they led him here. Psalm 103 is close to a perfect landing. "Do not forget all His kind deeds" sounds like the recovery habit of remembering where you came from, and the rest of the psalm ("who redeems your life from the pit", sins removed "as far as the east is from the west", a father's compassion for his children) speaks straight to his sobriety and his son being there. Athanasius's advice to "stir up your own soul" to bless God is exactly the urge he feels. Line 2 would also have fitted, but line 1 is the more direct match. Nothing pushed him into a box, and nothing about his drinking was named or assumed.

results.desc: Esther, 29, Kumasi, Ghana, Methodist. After two years of trying, she and her husband found out she is pregnant. She keeps thinking about all the months she prayed for this and feels that God really did hear her.

answers.wanted: Both 'Something new just began' and 'Something hard just ended' are true for her: two years of waiting ended and a pregnancy began. She'd want one option like 'Something I've waited a long time for finally happened'
The baby, or 'Something I've been praying for'. 'Someone I care about' is the nearest. 'God, and where I stand with Him' sounds like worry or guilt, not thankfulness, and 'My health' feels clinical
'That they're safe and healthy' or 'That they arrive safely'. All three options assume the person she cares about is suffering
'He answered my prayer', or 'Something I asked Him for, for a long time'. That option only appears behind 'Something hard just ended', so she never sees it

friction.note: 'Something hard just ended' and 'Something new just began' are not either/or. Anyone whose long wait ended in good news fits both, and which one she taps changes her follow-ups: the answered-prayer option is only on the 'ended' path.

The list has no option for a hope, a prayer, or something good you're waiting on. Almost every option is a problem. 'God, and where I stand with Him' reads like guilt or doubt, not a neutral option a thankful person would pick.

There is no 'Hopeful' or 'Excited', and nothing for joy mixed with nerves. That is very common in early pregnancy after years of trying: grateful but afraid it could still go wrong. Of the nine words, six are negative and three positive.

'Comfort / A way out, or healing / Someone to help them' assumes the person you care about is in trouble. If they're on your mind for a happy reason, it pushes you into the wrong answer. It needs a positive and a neutral option.

'A new home' and 'Someone coming to faith' feel hyper-specific, like boxes waiting for someone to fall in. The obvious reason a Christian says life is good, a prayer answered, is missing. 'How good and well-made everything is' sounds odd said out loud.
The seven options lean negative (against, talking, hard, gone) against three positive, with only 'Fine' in the middle. 'A real gift' vs 'Kind to me' is a hair-thin difference.
'Why do they get away with it?' and 'You decide who's right' are very specific grievances next to general options like 'Help.' and 'Thank You.' The list feels uneven.

results.overall: Most of the core questions went quickly for her and felt right: really good, grateful, God clearly at work, thank you. But the quiz never let her say the one thing that defines this season, that God answered a long prayer. The 'someone I care about' path then treated her unborn baby as someone in trouble, and she came away feeling her happy news had been squeezed into a list built for hard times.

verdict.why: As Esther I'd say yes to the first line straight away. Thanking God is exactly where I am. Psalm 103 speaks to me: "do not forget all His kind deeds", the God who "satisfies you with good things" and "redeems your life". It feels like a psalm for remembering all those months of prayer and seeing that He answered. The line is a bit general, though. It says "thank God" but not "He heard me", and hearing is the heart of how I feel. The words "in and through everything" also hint at hardship I'm not in right now. I'd feel seen, but only broadly, not recognised in particular. An answered-prayer line such as Psalm 116 ("He has heard my voice"), if Athanasius's letter names it, would feel like the quiz truly understood me. Line 2 (Psalm 145) would also fit. Line 3 (Psalm 20) would feel off, because I'm not comforting anyone. Nothing here would wound me.
verdict.theirSituation: After two years of prayer she is finally pregnant and is full of thanks that God heard her prayers, not just grateful in general.

results.desc: David, 35, Denver, Colorado, evangelical. He was promoted to regional manager, with a big raise and a team of twenty. He is thrilled and a bit wary of how much he wanted it, and he wants to stay humble and not let it take over his life.

answers.wanted: Excited, but a bit wary. Something like 'Thrilled' or 'Excited', or a way to say 'happy but careful'.
Something like 'Supportive' or 'Happy for me'. 'Kind to me' works, but it sounds like I needed looking after.
'Thank You, and keep me humble' or 'Keep me grounded.' The humility worry is the main thing on my mind, and none of the options let me say it.
'Things are going well at work' or 'Something I worked for came through.' 'I can see Him leading me' is near enough, but it's more spiritual than how I'd put it.

friction.note: The list has seven hard words (afraid, heavy, worn out, angry, numb, restless, calm) and only two happy ones. A happy person has little to choose from, and there's nothing for mixed feelings like 'excited but nervous'.

Most options are laments or complaints: how long, why do they get away with it, you decide who's right. A good season gets only 'Thank You' or 'How great You are'. There's nothing for asking for guidance, humility or wisdom in success ('Keep me humble', 'Show me what to do with this'), and that's exactly what this person would want to say. The wariness he feels about his own ambition has no place anywhere in the quiz.

'A new home' and 'Someone coming to faith' are oddly specific next to vague options like 'Everything, really'. They feel like they were written to lead to particular psalms. There's no plain option for a good thing at work, a milestone reached or something you worked for, and a promotion is probably the most common reason someone's life has just got good. 'How good and well-made everything is' reads strangely.
'Something I've done' is phrased negatively, as if it has to be a wrongdoing. Someone thinking about an achievement, or worried about their own motives, would hesitate over it.
The seven options run from 'Against me' to 'A real gift', but four of them are negative, so the list leans toward trouble.
'Displeased with me' feels heavy to see among only six choices. It's fine here but may feel loaded to a casual user.

results.overall: Taking it was quick and mostly easy, but it felt built for people who are struggling. David's real situation (a good new season and a worry about staying humble in it) had nowhere to land. He kept tapping the closest cheerful option and wondering whether the result would miss the point.

verdict.why: I'd say yes to the first line. I got promoted and I'm thrilled, and my first instinct as an evangelical is that this came from God and I should thank Him. Psalm 103:2's "do not forget all His kind deeds" also touches the thing I'm uneasy about: success can make you forget where it came from. But the line only covers the gratitude. It says nothing about the other half of me, which is wary of how badly I wanted this and wants to stay humble and keep work from taking over my life. I would have said yes a lot faster to something like "Something good happened and you want to keep your heart in the right place" (Psalm 131, "my heart is not proud"). "In and through everything" also reads like a line for someone in hard times, not for someone who just got good news, so it feels a bit generic. Still, it doesn't box me in or misread me. Psalm 23 would also have been a fine second choice. The fallback page (grinding, weighing, afraid) would be completely wrong for me, but I never get that far.
verdict.theirSituation: He just got a big promotion he wanted badly and is grateful for it, but he is wary that wanting it so much could make him proud or let work take over his life, and he wants to stay humble.

results.desc: Mei, 26, Singapore, Presbyterian. Her best friend from university, who she had talked with about faith for years, was baptised on Sunday. Mei cried the whole way through and has felt light and hopeful all week.

answers.wanted: Honestly just this week has been really good. The stretch overall is normal, but I feel light right now.
Something good just happened. "Something new just began" is about me, and it was my friend's new beginning, not mine.
Hopeful, or Joyful. Grateful is near but not quite the feeling.
For them to keep growing, or to stay close to God. Nothing's wrong with my friend. Something wonderful happened to her.

friction.note: Every option (Comfort, A way out or healing, Someone to help them) assumes the person I care about is in trouble. I tapped "Someone I care about" because of happy news, so this felt like the quiz decided my friend must be suffering. It needs a positive and a neutral option, e.g. "For them to keep growing" or "Just for them to be happy".
"Someone in my life" and "Someone I care about" read as the same thing. I had to guess which one meant the good kind.

All the options are about my own life. Nothing covers a good event in someone else's life that lifted me. "Something hard just ended" and "Something new just began" feel oddly specific next to the general ones.

The positive words (Calm, Grateful, Glad) are fewer and flatter than the negative ones (Afraid, Heavy, Worn out, Angry, Numb, Restless). There's no Hopeful or Joyful, so it tilts toward the hard side.
"This stretch of your life" is too broad when one recent event is driving how I feel. I wasn't sure whether to answer for the week or the year.
"A new home" sits oddly among the other options. "Someone coming to faith" fitted perfectly, but it's so exact that it gives away that the quiz is steering toward specific psalms.
Fine for me, but the list has seven hard options to two positive ones (Thank You, How great You are). A cheerful person has much less choice.

results.overall: The core questions went quickly and mostly fitted, though I kept picking the nearest word, not the right one. Then the follow-up about the person I care about assumed they were in trouble when my news was joyful, and that felt like being pushed into a sad story that wasn't mine.

verdict.why: As Mei I would probably say yes to line 1. I am overflowing with thanks this week, and "thank God, in and through everything" is close enough that I would tap "Yes, that's it" without waiting to see what comes next. Psalm 103 ("Bless the LORD, O my soul, and do not forget all His kind deeds") fits how I feel, so the result would land well. But line 3 is exactly me: I watched my friend be baptised after years of talking about faith, I cried all through it, and I am amazed at God's love. If line 3 had come first I would have felt truly seen, not just broadly matched. So the quiz knew my real situation and ranked a generic line above it. Line 1 is so broad that almost anyone who feels good would say yes to it. That hides the specific, surprising result that makes this quiz special (who knew Athanasius had a psalm for watching a baptism?). My suggestion is to rank the specific situation above the generic one when the answers point to it, or show the specific line with the general one as a fallback. Line 2 (poor and needy) has nothing to do with me, and nothing here would hurt me.
verdict.theirSituation: Mei is full of joy and thankfulness because a close friend she had talked with about faith for years was just baptised, and she is amazed at God's love. Line 3 names that exactly, but line 1 comes first and is general enough that she would accept it.

results.desc: Patrick, 78, Dublin, Ireland, Catholic. His health is decent for his age and the grandchildren were over all weekend. He is content, thinks about death now and then without fear, and feels God has been good to him over a long life.

answers.wanted: Content, or at peace. Grateful is true, but 'content' is the word he would actually use about himself
My family / the grandchildren, in a good way. Or 'getting older and what comes after', said without fear. 'Someone I care about' sounds like he is worried about them, so he would avoid it
A long life, and good people around me. 'His kindness' is near enough, but he would want something about looking back over the years and his family

friction.note: Every specific option is a worry: a person, a wrong, health, money, a loss, the world, standing with God. Add a warm, neutral choice such as 'My family' or 'The people I love', with no hint that something is wrong.

Of nine words, five are negative and only 'Calm', 'Grateful' and 'Glad' are good. There is no 'Content' or 'At peace', which is the most common state for someone like him.

'How good and well-made everything is' is stilted; he would say 'the world around me' or 'the simple things'.

'About the same' is fine, but it has no warm version of steady, such as 'Steady, and I'm glad of it'. Every other change option is dramatic ('Something hard just ended', 'Something new just began').

results.overall: For a contented older man it goes easily and quickly, and most taps are honest. But the middle questions lean toward trouble. He keeps looking for 'content', 'family' or 'getting on in years, and at peace with it' and has to settle for a shrug or a near word. The last follow-up throws up options that feel oddly specific to him ('A new home', 'I'm growing').

verdict.why: As Patrick, I would say yes to the first line. He is content, grateful for a long life, and has just had the grandchildren over all weekend. Wanting to thank God in and through everything is exactly where he is, and "do not forget all His kind deeds" reads like his own looking-back. Psalm 103 fits a 78-year-old especially well. Its later verses say our days are like grass but the LORD's steadfast love is from everlasting to everlasting on those who fear Him, and to their children's children. That speaks to him thinking about death without fear and to his grandchildren, without the quiz having to ask about either. Line 2 would also have landed, so the grateful and content path works for him from either line. He would feel seen, not boxed in.

results.desc: Milica, 49, Belgrade, Serbia, Orthodox. The fasting season she kept this summer went better than any before, and she feels clear-headed and calm. Work is steady and the family is well; she mostly wants to hold on to the quiet she found.

answers.wanted: Calmer and steadier than before. It is less 'getting better' and more 'settled'. Something good I did just ended, the fast, and I want to keep what it gave me.
Holding on to the peace I've found. 'Where I stand with Him' sounds like I'm worried about it, and I'm not.
Something between 'Fine' and 'Kind to me', like 'Good, all well'. 'Fine' sounds colder than my family has been.
A season of prayer and fasting that went well / A peace I want to keep. 'I'm growing' sounds a bit self-satisfied, and 'I can see Him leading me' is too strong for a quiet time.

friction.note: For a calm person nothing fits comfortably. 'Nothing in particular' sounds empty, and 'God, and where I stand with Him' reads as anxious. There is no calm or positive option such as 'Keeping hold of something good' or 'Being thankful'. Most of the options are problems.
Six of the nine words are negative and only three are positive, and there is nothing in between (settled, hopeful, content, at peace). A calm person has to scan past a list of troubles.

results.overall: The quiz went quickly and felt pleasant for the first three questions. After that, Milica kept looking past answers written for people in trouble and settling for 'close enough'. The quiz seems built for hard times, and a calm, thankful person gets few options that sound like her.

verdict.why: Milica would say "Yes, that's it" to the first line. Her summer fast went better than ever, work and family are well, and she feels calm. Thanks is the natural response, and "bless the LORD, O my soul, and do not forget all His kind deeds" fits someone afraid of losing a good season. The second line ("climbing") would also fit, because the fast felt like progress, but she would stop at the first. It is not exact. What she mainly wants is to keep the quiet she found, and neither line names that. "Do not forget His kind deeds" comes close, which is why it works well enough. verdict.theirSituation: She is in a calm, grateful season after a fast that went well, and what she wants most is to guard that quiet, not just to give thanks.

results.desc: Jorge, 44, Bogotá, Colombia, evangelical. A former business partner who cheated him lost the court case this month, and Jorge's small printing business has finally paid off its debts. He feels vindicated and relieved, and grateful that he didn't take matters into his own hands.

answers.wanted: Relieved (grateful fits too, but relief is the first word he'd reach for)
How a wrong done to me finally got put right (the court case against his ex-partner); he split between 'Someone in my life' and 'Work, money' and neither is quite it
Someone was against me, but that's over now / most people have been kind, one wasn't
Someone who wronged me (one person, not 'people')
I left it in His hands and justice was done / I didn't take revenge, and He settled it

friction.note: Every option is about right now. Nothing covers 'someone was against me, but that's finished', so a person whose conflict just ended is forced into 'Fine' and the quiz loses the most important fact about his story.
'Someone in my life' is a strange fit for a former business partner who cheated him; it sounds like family or a friend. There's no 'something unfair that got settled' or 'justice' option.
'People who were against me' is plural and sounds like a crowd or a feud; he had one opponent. 'A time God felt against me' sounds heavy and unfamiliar to an ordinary evangelical.

No option for 'I waited and didn't take revenge, and it was put right', which is exactly what he's grateful for. 'I kept my head and got away' reads like fleeing, and 'It just passed' feels flippant. 'He corrected me, gently' feels out of place in a list about how trouble ended.
No 'Relieved', which is the most common feeling after something hard ends. The list jumps from negative words to 'Calm/Grateful/Glad'.

Skipped because trend was 'ended', but he is grateful and his business is finally out of debt. A 'what's behind it' question (for example 'God provided') would have fit him, and he never got asked it.
'Why do they get away with it?' and 'You decide who's right' are very specific and read like hints at a certain psalm. Mixing them in beside 'Thank You' feels unbalanced.

results.overall: Fast, and mostly easy for Jorge, but the questions keep asking about the present or about trouble, so his real story (a wrong that has just been put right, and that he didn't avenge) only fits sideways. He ended up with three 'close' answers on the questions that matter most.

verdict.why: Line 1 is close to Jorge's month: someone close turned on him, he prayed, the court ruled for him, and he wants to thank God. Psalm 4:1, "You have relieved my distress", fits both the court win and the paid-off debts. Psalm 4:3, "the LORD hears when I call to Him", is the vindication he feels. The same psalm's "in your anger do not sin" also fits his thankfulness that he didn't take revenge, although the card doesn't show that verse. The one weak spot is "your own people". Many readers will take that to mean family or his church, not a business partner, so he may pause before tapping yes. Line 2 would also be true of him, but it is too general to feel personal. It is a good second choice, but line 1 is the one that names what happened.
verdict.theirSituation: A former business partner cheated Jorge. This month the partner lost the court case, and Jorge's business finished paying off its debts. He feels vindicated and relieved, and he is grateful to God that he didn't take revenge himself.

results.desc: Abigail, 21, Cape Town, South Africa, Anglican. University is going well, she has a new boyfriend she really likes, and she has good friends around her. She's busy and happy and thanks God often, though mostly on the run.

answers.wanted: Getting better, AND something new began. It's a new relationship, not one big event, so I hesitated between 'better' and 'new'
Happy. Nobody my age says 'glad'. I also nearly tapped 'Grateful', and I'd have liked 'Excited'
My boyfriend, or a new relationship. 'Someone in my life' sounded like it could mean trouble, so I picked 'Someone I care about'. Uni ('what's next') was a close second
Close, though I don't stop to feel it much. Something like 'Good, I just don't slow down enough'
Nothing's wrong with him. I'd want 'That it keeps going well', 'That we grow together' or 'Just that they're happy'. Every option here assumes the person is suffering

The people in my life, meaning a new relationship and good friends, plus uni going well. None of the specific options (a new home, someone coming to faith, His leading) covers ordinary good things like love, friends and studies

'Something hard just ended' and 'Something new just began' mix two different things (a direction and an event) into a scale that otherwise runs worse, same, better. You can easily be both 'better' and 'new'.
This one is fairly balanced, but 'Clearly at work' and 'Close' blur together, and there's nothing for 'good, but I'm too busy to notice much', which is honestly where a lot of happy, busy people are.

results.overall: It was quick and mostly pleasant, and 'Really good', 'Kind to me' and 'Thank You' felt natural. But as a happy person I kept wading through lists built for people who are struggling. verdict.why: Abigail is happy and thanks God often, so "You want to thank God, in and through everything" fits her, and Psalm 103:2 ("Bless the LORD, O my soul, and do not forget all His kind deeds") is the psalm she would recognise as hers right now. She would say "Not quite" to line 1 without much trouble: nobody she loves is in trouble. But it is telling that a trouble-shaped line came first for someone whose life is going this well. That backs up the owner's complaint that the questions lean toward the negative and leave no clean neutral or positive route. "In and through everything" also hints at hardship she isn't going through, and it misses the lightness of "thanks God often, though mostly on the run". A line such as "Life is good right now, and you keep catching yourself saying thank You" would describe her exactly.
verdict.wouldHurt: Nothing would wound her. Seeing a "someone you love is in trouble" line ranked first when her life is good could feel a little misread, as if the quiz assumes everyone arrives with a problem.
verdict.theirSituation: Life is simply good (studies going well, a new relationship, close friends), and her thanks are quick and frequent, not thanks through hardship.

I said I am grateful and things are good, yet I never got the 'What's behind it?' question, because I chose 'Something hard just ended'. The joyful side of my answer is never explored, and the follow-ups only ask about the trouble.

But once I said something hard had ended, the follow-ups assumed enemies and rescue. verdict.why: As Kenji, line 1 reaches for my situation but overstates it. A colleague being cold for a year is not "my own people turned against me", and I didn't really cry out to the Lord about it. The phrase makes a small office chill sound like betrayal by family or church, so I'd tap "Not quite". Line 2, "You want to thank God, in and through everything", is true of me today: quiet gratitude, seeing His hand in a small thing. Psalm 103's "Bless the LORD, O my soul, and do not forget all His kind deeds" fits how I feel. The line itself says nothing about peace being restored between people, so it lands near enough rather than exactly. The psalm does help: its later lines about God not staying angry forever would speak to the reconciliation if I read on. Note for the quiz: line 1 is the right family (a relationship healed, now thanks), but "your own people turned against you" is too dramatic for the ordinary small repair many people will have. A gentler wording, such as "Things were strained with someone close to you, and now they're mended. You see God in it and want to thank Him", would catch far more people. That may also mean a separate result for reconciliation.
verdict.wouldHurt: Nothing wounding. Line 1's "your own people turned against you" misreads a cooled working relationship as hostility, and it could feel like it makes too much of what happened.
verdict.theirSituation: A colleague who was cold to him for a year made peace with him over dinner, and he feels a quiet, grateful joy and sees God's hand in the reconciliation.

results.desc: Leah, 31, Portland, Oregon, returning after years away from church. She feels welcomed, a little surprised at herself, and closer to God than she has in a long time.

answers.wanted: Both 'Getting better' and 'Something new just began' fit, and I had to pick one. Four months back at church is something new AND things getting better. I'd have liked to tap both, or see something like 'Something new began, and it's going well'.
'Coming back to God' or 'My faith, and finding my way back'. 'Where I stand with Him' sounds like I'm being graded or worried about my standing. I'm not worried, I'm just happily thinking about Him.

'Coming back to Him' or 'Finding a church that feels like home'. 'Someone coming to faith' sounds like it means another person, so it doesn't feel like it's about me coming back. 'A new home' could mean my church, but it reads like I moved house, so I didn't tap it.

friction.note: Nothing here fits someone who has come back to faith. 'Someone coming to faith' reads as another person getting saved, and a returner wouldn't see herself in it. 'A new home' is unclear: is it a house or a church? For someone in my position, either one could be the true answer.

'God, and where I stand with Him' leans toward worry or judgment. Someone who is happily close to God has no neutral-to-positive way to say 'God has been on my mind'. Something like 'God, and my faith' would cover both the worried and the happy.

'Getting better' and 'Something new just began' overlap for anyone whose good stretch began with a change. I couldn't tell whether the quiz wanted the cause or the direction. 'Just' also doesn't fit four months ago.

Mostly fine for me, but it has 7 heavy options against 2 positive ones (Thank You, How great You are). A happy person can find their answer, but the list feels like it expects trouble. It would help to have one quieter positive, like 'Stay close' or 'I'm glad I came back'.
The list fit me, but it has 6 negative words against 3 positive and no neutral like 'Hopeful' or 'Content'. 'Hopeful' would fit a lot of people who are starting over.

results.overall: The quiz was quick and mostly easy, and the core questions let a happy person answer honestly. But at the two moments that mattered most for my story (what's on my mind, and what's behind the good stretch), there was no option for coming back to faith, so I had to pick the nearest one. It left me feeling a little pushed into someone else's story right at the end.

verdict.why: As Leah, the first line would get a yes, but not a strong one. Four months in, what I mostly feel is grateful, so "You want to thank God" fits. "In and through everything" pulls a little toward thanking God through hard times, which isn't where I am. I'm on the good side of things right now, so the line sounds slightly more tested and grown-up than I feel. Psalm 103:2, "do not forget all His kind deeds", would land warmly for someone who forgot Him for a decade and is now remembering. Honestly, the second line fits better: being guided back, finding a church that feels like home, and being glad about it is Psalm 23. Because the thanks line is shown first and is close enough, I would take it and never see the one that fits best. Neither line catches the heart of my situation: coming back after years away, and being surprised at myself. That is the part I'd most want the quiz to notice. The fallback ("grinding me down", "weighing on me", "afraid") would have been completely wrong for me, and it frames the quiz as if life must be hard.
verdict.theirSituation: She has come back to God and church after years of drifting, and what she feels is glad gratitude and a sense of being led home. She is not thanking Him through hardship.
